title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel: From Climate Imperative To Strategic Asset | Aerospace Defense Outlook
authors: Dr.Ulrike Ziegler, President, Impact on Sustainable Aviation, Dr.Ulrike Ziegler, Impact on Sustainable Aviation
description:

According to the SkyNRG & ICF SAF Market Outlook 2026[1], global SAF production doubled again in 2025 to approximately two million tonnes.
Countries with access to sustainable feedstocks or renewable power will be able to develop strategic advantages in future aviation fuel markets.

Nations that succeed in building diversified aviation fuel ecosystems will strengthen both their aerospace sectors and their strategic resilience.
text:
Liquid fuels will remain central to aviation

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) entered the aviation debate as a climate solution. It is increasingly becoming something more consequential: an industrial capability with implications for energy security, supply chain resilience and military readiness. For aerospace and defense leaders, the key question is no longer whether if and what role SAF will play in the future, but whether sufficient production capacity can be built before fuel availability becomes a strategic constraint.

The reason is straightforward. Long-haul aviation remains fundamentally dependent on liquid hydrocarbons. While electric propulsion may find applications in smaller aircraft and hydrogen could eventually support parts of the market, both face significant technical and infrastructure hurdles at scale. For the aircraft that transport passengers, cargo, military personnel and critical equipment across continents, liquid fuels will remain indispensable for decades.

As Valentin Batteiger of Bauhaus Luftfahrt has argued at our recent IMPACT Aviation Stocktake Forum 2026, even optimistic hydrogen scenarios continue to require substantial volumes of drop-in liquid fuels throughout the transition. The challenge facing aviation, therefore, is not simply how to reduce emissions, but how to secure sufficient quantities of sustainable liquid fuel while maintaining affordability, reliability and operational flexibility.

This reality has made SAF the focal point of aviation’s decarbonization efforts. Unlike many alternative propulsion technologies, SAF can be used in today’s aircraft, engines and fueling infrastructure. Airlines do not need to replace fleets, airports do not need to rebuild fuel systems, and operators can integrate SAF into existing logistics networks. The technology challenge, in large part, has already been solved. The task now is deployment at scale.

Demand is growing faster than supply

The market is responding. According to the SkyNRG & ICF SAF Market Outlook 2026[1], global SAF production doubled again in 2025 to approximately two million tonnes. Demand is expected to accelerate sharply over the remainder of the decade, driven by increasingly stringent regulatory requirements and corporate decarbonization commitments. In Europe, ReFuelEU Aviation and the UK’s SAF mandate have transformed SAF from a voluntary environmental initiative into a compliance market supported by long-term demand signals.

Demand, however, is only one side of the equation.

The more pressing challenge is building a fuel supply system capable of supporting sustained growth. Today’s SAF market has largely been built on Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA), a production pathway that converts used cooking oil, animal fats and other lipid feedstocks into aviation fuel. HEFA is an instrumental building block on the road to commercial scale of and deserves much of the credit for the industry’s progress to date.

At the same time, HEFA is unlikely to provide a complete long-term solution. Feedstocks are inherently limited, and competition for those resources is increasing across multiple sectors. Nearly 85% of announced SAF production capacity still relies on HEFA pathways, raising concerns about future supply constraints as demand accelerates. Both Batteiger’s statement and the SkyNRG & ICF outlook point to a growing need for diversification into alcohol-to-jet, Fischer-Tropsch, advanced biofuel and synthetic e-fuel pathways if SAF is to meet long-term aviation demand.

In many respects, the industry’s next challenge is not scaling SAF production alone, but broadening the range of technologies and feedstocks that support it.

Why fuel diversification matters

That challenge has direct implications for resilience.

Recent years – further emphasized by the Iran war in early 2026 – have underscored the vulnerability of global energy markets to geopolitical shocks, supply disruptions and trade tensions. Aviation – in particularly in Europe, Asia and Oceania – remains heavily reliant on fossil fuel imports. Diversifying fuel supply does not eliminate those risks, but it can reduce dependence on a limited set of resources and supply routes.

For governments, domestic SAF production increasingly represents an opportunity to strengthen industrial capacity while reducing exposure to external energy shocks. Countries with access to sustainable feedstocks or renewable power will be able to develop strategic advantages in future aviation fuel markets. As a result, SAF is increasingly being discussed not only in climate ministries but also in departments responsible for industry, energy and national security.

Until recently, calls for military SAF procurement were often framed as a way for governments to support the development of an emerging industry. The objective was to help create the long-term demand signals needed to unlock investment in first-of-a-kind production facilities. Recent geopolitical developments have broadened that perspective. What was once primarily viewed as industrial support is increasingly regarded as an investment in fuel resilience, supply security and long-term operational readiness.

The defense sector has a direct take

The defense community has a particular stake in this discussion.

Fuel availability has always been a readiness issue. Military aviation depends on assured access to liquid fuels for airlift, surveillance, aerial refueling, logistics support and operational deployment. Range, endurance and reliability remain essential requirements, and any future aviation fuel system must meet those standards under demanding operational conditions.

Historically, defense organizations have often played an important role in helping emerging technologies reach scale. SAF presents a similar opportunity. While military demand alone will not determine the market’s trajectory, defense institutions can provide something that many first-of-a-kind projects struggle to secure: credible, long-term demand.

For project developers and financiers, uncertainty remains a major obstacle. Large SAF facilities require substantial upfront investment, yet investors continue to seek stronger certainty around future revenues and market stability. Long-term procurement commitments from highly creditworthy buyers can help reduce those risks, improve project bankability and send a much-needed signal in support of SAF beyond mere policies.

Military operators can also contribute in another important way: demonstrating operational confidence. Successful SAF deployments validate fuel performance under demanding conditions and help build trust across the wider aviation ecosystem. Every operational use case provides additional evidence for airlines, regulators, financiers and policymakers that SAF can support real-world missions at scale.

From demonstration to industrial scale

The broader strategic benefit is diversification. A future fuel ecosystem that combines conventional refining capacity, advanced biofuels and synthetic fuels sourced from a variety of feedstocks is likely to be more robust than one dependent on a narrow set of fossil-fuel supply chains. Greater diversity in production pathways can strengthen resilience against market disruptions, geopolitical tensions and resource constraints.

Achieving that outcome will require collaboration far beyond the fuel sector itself. Airlines and corporate buyers of SAF certificates cannot solve the challenge independently. Nor can fuel producers, governments or investors acting in isolation. Building a mature SAF market requires coordinated action across aircraft manufacturers, engine companies, airports, energy suppliers, financial institutions, defense organizations and policymakers. Success will depend on aligning capital, technology, regulation and demand.

For aerospace and defense leaders, SAF should therefore be viewed through multiple lenses at once. It remains aviation’s most important near-term decarbonization tool. It represents an industrial opportunity capable of creating new value chains and attracting investment. Last but not least, it also contributes to a broader conversation about RESILIENCE, preparedness and long-term fuel security.

An investment in future readiness

The coming years will determine whether SAF develops into a scalable global fuel industry or remains constrained by feedstock limitations and financing bottlenecks. The underlying technologies exist. Demand is steadily strengthening. The remaining task is to mobilize the investment, infrastructure and market confidence required for industrial-scale deployment.

SAF will continue to be discussed through the lens of emissions reduction, and rightly so. Yet the next phase of the story will be shaped just as much by questions of supply, capability and industrial capacity. Nations that succeed in building diversified aviation fuel ecosystems will strengthen both their aerospace sectors and their strategic resilience. For defense organizations, supporting that transition is not simply an environmental choice. It is an investment in future operational readiness.

text:
The United States is working to reduce its reliance on petroleum-based aviation fuel by increasing the use of sustainable aviation fuel derived from renewable resources by 2050. A Rowan University research team is studying ways to produce these fuels.

Jun Hee Jang, Ph.D., an assistant professor of chemical engineering in the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering, received a $199,999 grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation to study a sustainable and cost-effective process for converting biomass into jet fuel. The grant was awarded through NSF's Engineering Research Initiation (ERI) program, which supports engineering faculty at emerging research institutions as they establish independent research programs.

Aviation fuel is a blend of compounds, including linear and branched hydrocarbons and aromatic compounds. Researchers have developed well-established processes for converting biomass such as vegetable oils into hydrocarbons. However, aromatic compounds are typically derived from petroleum. Jang’s research will examine lignin, a natural polymer derived from woody biomass, as a sustainable aromatic alternative for aviation fuels.

If successful, the approach could help expand domestic production of sustainable aviation fuel while creating additional value from biomass feedstocks that might otherwise go unused.

To do so, Jang and his team must first break lignin into smaller molecules. This process produces a mixture of smaller molecules that can be upgraded into aviation fuel components and larger molecules that cannot. However, efficiently separating the smaller molecules from the larger ones is challenging. Jang and his team will develop a size-selective catalyst that allows only the smaller molecules to enter its porous structure, where they can be converted into jet fuel-range aromatic compounds, while preventing larger molecules from entering.

While the smaller molecules can be converted into aviation fuel components, the larger molecules retain properties that may make them useful for other applications. In conventional catalysis processes, these larger molecules are waste products. This approach, however, could create a valuable co-product rather than waste.

“By applying this catalyst, we can produce not only fuel aromatics, but also larger molecules that could have further functional applications,” Jang said. “We are making two products out of the same feedstock.”

Jang will be joined on this project by one doctoral student and one postdoctoral researcher. The postdoctoral researcher has experience designing chemical synthesis methods. The doctoral student will conduct experiments and analyze the resulting products. Together, the team will study how catalyst design influences reaction performance. The team also will evaluate the economic viability of scaling the proposed biomass-to-aviation fuel process using the new size-selective catalysts.

text:
Synopsis

India's Sustainable Aviation Fuel readiness is estimated at 52 percent, showing moderate progress in adoption. The country aims for blending targets of 1 percent by 2027 and 5 percent by 2030. A coordinated approach among stakeholders is essential for developing the Sustainable Aviation Fuel market. The report highlights India's potential in supporting sustainable aviation amid growing aviation demand.

Mumbai: India's overall Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) readiness is estimated to be around 52 per cent, indicating moderate but advancing readiness as the country moves from early-stage development towards wider SAF adoption, a report said on Tuesday.

The joint report by US aircraft major Boeing and Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB) also shows that India's opportunity will depend not only on production potential, but on the coordinated development of the wider enabling ecosystem.

India has set blending targets of 1 per cent by 2027, 2 per cent by 2028 and eventually 5 per cent by 2030.

The country is also committed to participating in the International Civil Aviation Organization's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) from 2027.

Live Events

Under a 5 per cent blending scenario in 2030, SAF demand covering both domestic and international aviation is projected at approximately 720 million litres (about 0.6 million tonnes per year), compared with an estimated production potential of 14-33 million tonnes per year, as per the report.

The report carries out a comprehensive assessment of India's readiness for SAF adoption, providing an evidence-based roadmap for the country's next phase of SAF development.

Read more: Air India's new chief sets sights on higher revenue and cost curbs at first town hall

"The report finds India's overall SAF readiness to be 52 per cent, indicating moderate but advancing readiness as the country moves from early-stage development toward wider SAF adoption," it said.

The report examines and uncovers strengths and opportunities in India's SAF adoption journey, as aviation demand continues to grow. It has been developed by RSB using a methodology which evaluates India's preparedness across nine dimensions - feedstock, production capacity, policy and regulation, supply chains and logistics, market demand, investment and financing, research and development, technology readiness, and enabling infrastructure and services.

"As one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets, India has an important role in enabling sustainable aviation and pursuing a deliberate and well-researched path to SAF adoption is key," said Salil Gupte, president, Boeing India and South Asia.

"This report is valuable because it confirms exactly where India has the foundational capacity to enable SAF adoption and because it identifies specific opportunities ahead," Gupte added.

Aligned with the industry, the report stated, Boeing is committed to supporting airline customers and policymakers in India and globally in achieving their emissions reduction goals by helping to build a robust SAF ecosystem.

"India's Sustainable Aviation Fuel opportunity is substantial. This assessment gives stakeholders a common evidence base from which to act, and RSB looks forward to continuing to convene and support the collaboration needed to translate India's potential into sustainable impact," said RSB's Executive Director, Bettina Paschke.

Coordinated action and collaboration across government, industry, financiers, and other stakeholders will be important to support the development of the SAF market in India, it stated.

text:
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources (MOTIR, Minister JK Kim) will host the second round of negotiations for the Green Economy Partnership Agreement (GEPA) in Seoul from September 30 to October 2, 2026. In negotiating this plurilateral agreement, participating countries will discuss trade rules for the green economy and cooperative measures to expand trade and investment.

The Office of Trade Negotiations at MOTIR said around 20 delegates from Korea, New Zealand, Singapore and Chile will participate in the negotiations. New Zealand, Singapore and Chile previously announced plans to pursue GEPA on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in October 2025 and subsequently launched negotiations in Singapore in July 2026. Korea formalized its participation in GEPA through an exchange of letters between the trade ministers on September 11, 2026, and will now take part in the negotiations beginning with this second round.

GEPA aims to establish common standards among participating countries for trade-related climate measures such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and facilitate trade in low-emission goods, including low-carbon steel. This round of negotiations will focus on criteria for identifying low-emission and environmental goods, measures to expand trade in these products, and cooperation on the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in the aviation sector.

description:
New Delhi: India is making steady progress towards adopting Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), according to a new report by Boeing and the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB).
The report gives India an overall SAF readiness score of 52 per cent.
The assessment is based on conditions prevailing around the middle of 2026 and is intended as a measure of India's domestic readiness.
Its feedstock readiness is assessed at 78 per cent, while SAF production capacity and technology readiness each score 60 per cent.

text:
New Delhi:

India is making steady progress towards adopting Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), according to a new report by Boeing and the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB). However, the report added that India's ability to move from ambition to large-scale production remains constrained by gaps in policy and infrastructure, among other things.

The report gives India an overall SAF readiness score of 52 per cent. The assessment is based on conditions prevailing around the middle of 2026 and is intended as a measure of India's domestic readiness.

The findings come as India prepares for an expansion of its aviation sector while also seeking to reduce the carbon intensity of air travel. India has indicated blending targets of 1 per cent SAF by 2027, 2 per cent by 2028 and 5 per cent by 2030, while entering the mandatory phase of the International Civil Aviation Organization's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) from 2027.

The report says India's challenge is not primarily a shortage of potential feedstock or technical capability. Instead, the harder task will be building the system needed to turn that potential into a dependable commercial supply of fuel.

Its feedstock readiness is assessed at 78 per cent, while SAF production capacity and technology readiness each score 60 per cent. Policy and regulation scores 53 per cent, while research and development is at 50 per cent. The weaker areas are supply chain and logistics at 45 per cent, investment and financing at 40 per cent, enabling infrastructure and services at 40 per cent, and market demand at just 30 per cent.

India's theoretical SAF production potential is estimated in the report at 14 million to 33 million tonnes a year, based on available feedstock resources. By comparison, SAF demand under a 5 per cent blending scenario covering both domestic and international aviation is projected at about 720 million litres a year by 2030, equivalent to roughly 0.6 million tonnes.

That gap reveals that India has considerable resource potential relative to its near-term requirement. The problem is getting those resources into the production system reliably.

Another key finding in the report is that India's SAF challenge lies less in whether the country can produce the fuel and more in whether it can create the conditions that make production commercially viable.

Policy along with R&D are assessed as areas showing progress and strategic intent. But investment and financing, market demand, and enabling infrastructure and services are identified as particularly weak areas.

text:
Milestone validates Aether's integrated technology platform at larger scale and advances the company toward commercial deployment of next-generation sustainable aviation fuel

RESEARCH TRIANGLE PARK, N.C. and CHICAGO, Sept. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aether Fuels Inc. (Aether), a sustainable fuels technology company, announced the successful construction, commissioning, and operation of its fully integrated demonstration line, including the production of synthetic aviation fuel which meets the specifications of ASTM D7566, the international standard for synthetic jet fuel. This is a major milestone in the commercialization of its Aether Aurora™ technology platform.

This demonstration line utilized Aether's 2.5 barrel-per-day capacity Aether Aurora Tri-Converter and Aurora Upgrader units, integrated together with RTI's existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor. The fuel was produced using mass-balanced renewable natural gas (RNG) derived from landfill gas generated in Kentucky and industrial CO2 as feedstocks and included the complete conversion process from waste-derived gas feedstocks to fully upgraded synthetic liquid jet fuel. Aether is believed to be the first company in North America to produce ASTM-specification synthetic aviation fuel from mass-balanced RNG and captured industrial CO2 at this scale.

Independent third-party testing conducted by AmSpec (www.amspecgroup.com) confirmed that the fuel samples produced during this demo run met the applicable ASTM specifications for FT-SPK (Annex A1 for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK)). Under the ASTM D7566 standard, alternative fuels meeting this specification are approved for blending with conventional kerosene up to 50% without requiring modifications to existing aircraft tanks, pipelines, or airport fueling systems. Additionally, because the FT-SPK route is already approved under the ASTM, no new ASTM certification is required.

"This demonstration proves Aether's ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel. It is the culmination of over a year of hard work by Aether's R&D team and is a tremendous milestone," said Dhaval Shah, Chief Technology Officer of Aether Fuels. "Just as importantly, the data from this demonstration informs and de-risks the design of our 50 BPD Project Beacon plant in Singapore, as we continue rapid journey to large scale commercial deployment"

Building Toward Commercial Deployment

The demonstration builds on Aether's previously reported stand-alone demonstration of the Tri-Converter unit with GTI Energy and represents the latest step in Aether's progression from the lab to commercial deployment, and represents important technical validation ahead of Project Beacon, Aether's planned 2,000 metric tons per year (50 barrels per day) commercial project in Singapore.

Aether has a pipeline of large commercial projects under development that will follow Project Beacon and produce ASTM D7566-compliant sustainable aviation fuel with lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions of over 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.

"This is exciting progress for Aether as we march forward towards commercial deployment," said Conor Madigan, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Aether Fuels. "We started by systematically demonstrating each part of the Aurora platform at the pilot scale, then scaled our novel technology up more than 50X in standalone demo units, and in this most recent demonstration, brought these demo units together in an integrated line that produces ASTM spec jet fuel. This is a significant achievement and puts us on the right track to successfully build and operate Project Beacon and the commercial projects that will follow."

About Aether Fuels

Aether Fuels is a climate technology company revolutionizing sustainable fuel production to help hard-to-abate industries like aviation and ocean shipping achieve their decarbonization goals. Our breakthrough Aether Aurora™ technology converts waste carbon into drop-in liquid fuels with near-ideal carbon conversion efficiency. The scalable solution addresses the core requirements of next-generation sustainable fuels by increasing production yields and reducing capital costs, while utilizing a diverse range of feedstocks. title: China's SAF Exports Reach Record High as Europe's Demand Accelerates - ResourceWise
description:
Why Did China's SAF Exports Reach a Record High in August?
The country accounted for nearly three-quarters of all Chinese SAF exports during August.
August's performance provides further evidence that SAF trade is progressing beyond isolated cargoes toward larger and more consistent commercial flows.
Europe's near-total share of Chinese SAF exports reflects the region's growing role as a center of mandated SAF demand.
Follow the SAF Market's Next Moves Record trade volumes are one sign of a growing SAF market.
text:
China's sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) exports reached an all-time high in August, reinforcing the upward trend in shipments seen throughout 2026 and offering an encouraging signal for the market's continued development.

China exported approximately 131,000 tons of SAF during the month according to customs data. That was 37% higher than July's total and 30% above the previous monthly record set in May. It was also approximately 63% above the average monthly export volume recorded from January through August.

Europe received every ton exported in August, extending a pattern that has held since April. While a single record month does not define the market's long-term direction, the latest data shows that SAF is moving across borders at increasingly meaningful volumes. And European demand remains the central outlet for Chinese supply.

Why Did China's SAF Exports Reach a Record High in August?

The August record was driven primarily by a sharp increase in shipments to Belgium and alongside new highs in shipments to Spain and France.

Belgium received 62% more than in July and well above the record it had set just one month earlier. The country accounted for nearly three-quarters of all Chinese SAF exports during August.

Shipments to Spain rose 47% month over month to a new record. France also set a monthly record in August after taking no Chinese SAF in July.

These gains more than offset a steep decline in shipments to the Netherlands, which fell near 85% month-over-month from July to August. China has not exported SAF to the United Kingdom since May.

The shifts among individual destinations show that monthly trade routes can remain fluid even as the overall export trend strengthens. Volumes may move between European entry points based on multiple factors:

Purchasing activity

Logistics

Storage

Certification requirements

Other commercial considerations

The more important market-level development is that aggregate shipments continued to climb.

What Does the New Record Signal for the SAF Market?

August's performance provides further evidence that SAF trade is progressing beyond isolated cargoes toward larger and more consistent commercial flows.

Europe received 99.98% of China's export volume from January to August, making the connection between Chinese supply and European demand one of the clearest SAF trade relationships to emerge in 2026.

The pace of growth is particularly notable. August exports were higher than both the previous month and the earlier record. They were substantially above the year-to-date monthly average.

According to a Prima CarbonZero market report, the data indicates an acceleration in physical market activity.

For a sector working to scale production, establish dependable trade routes, and translate policy ambition into fuel consumption, rising cross-border volumes are an encouraging sign. They indicate that suppliers are placing larger quantities into the market and that buyers are finding channels to absorb them.

Why Is Europe Taking Nearly All of China's SAF?

Europe's near-total share of Chinese SAF exports reflects the region's growing role as a center of mandated SAF demand.

As aviation decarbonization requirements expand, European market participants must secure eligible fuel, understand available supply pathways, and manage the cost and compliance implications of rising demand. Chinese production has become an increasingly important source within that supply picture.

This concentration highlights both momentum and exposure. Europe is demonstrating a strong appetite for imported SAF. However, China's exports remain heavily dependent on a single region (and a small number of major destinations within that region). Changes in policy, eligibility rules, certification, trade measures, or buying patterns could therefore quickly redirect flows.

Is the Upward Trend in Chinese SAF Exports Sustainable?

The export trajectory is positive, but its durability will depend on more than production growth alone.

Future trade volumes will be shaped by several elements:

European mandate demand

Eligibility of Chinese supply under regional sustainability frameworks

Feedstock availability

Production economics

Competition from other suppliers

The movement of volumes among Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain, and France also shows why individual destination data should be interpreted within the broader trade picture.

Nevertheless, August represents a meaningful milestone. Chinese SAF exports have reached a new high, Europe continues to absorb virtually all available volume, and shipments are running well above their average pace for the year.

That does not eliminate the challenges facing SAF scale-up. It does, however, provide tangible evidence that the market is moving in the direction policymakers, producers, and aviation buyers have been working toward. This means greater supply, larger traded volumes, and increasingly established links between production centers and demand markets.

Follow the SAF Market's Next Moves

Record trade volumes are one sign of a growing SAF market. But they are only part of the picture.

Policy and mandate developments, pricing movements, feedstock economics, production activity, and shifting trade flows will all influence where the market goes next.

text:
SkyNRG has announced the selection of Technip Energies, Sasol, and Topsoe as key partners for the initial engineering activities of the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) phase of Project Wigeon, its planned sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility at the Port of Walla Walla in Washington State, US.

The appointments bring together technology and engineering expertise to support Project Wigeon as it progresses into FEED, a key phase in further developing the project’s engineering, cost, and execution plans towards a future Final Investment Decision (FID). Project Wigeon is designed to produce 50 million gal./yr (143 000 tpy) of SAF using renewable natural gas (RNG) and commercially proven Fischer-Tropsch technology. With key permitting secured and start-up targeted for 2031, the project aims to add significant new SAF production capacity in North America.

Topsoe and Sasol have each signed a Basic Engineering Design Package agreement with SkyNRG, providing technology licenses, engineering design, and technical services for their respective technologies. Project Wigeon will combine Topsoe’s SynCOR™ and hydroprocessing technologies with Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch technology to convert RNG into SAF.

Technip Energies brings extensive experience working with both Topsoe’s and Sasol’s technologies, alongside strong modularisation capabilities to support the project’s execution. The appointment also builds on SkyNRG’s established relationship with Technip Energies through DSL-01, SkyNRG’s SAF production facility currently under construction in Delfzijl, the Netherlands.

Steve Drennan, Co-President and Project Director: “Bringing Technip Energies, Sasol, and Topsoe on board is an important step in progressing Project Wigeon toward FEED. Together, we are combining proven technologies with deep engineering and project execution expertise to further develop a permitted, design-ready project and lay the foundations for commercial-scale advanced SAF production in the US.”

Loïc Chapuis, President Project Delivery and Services at Technip Energies, commented: “Project Wigeon marks a new step in our collaboration with SkyNRG, building on the work already underway on DSL-01 project in the Netherlands. This new milestone demonstrates how our engineering and project delivery expertise can support SkyNRG as it develops SAF projects across different geographies and contributes to the growth of sustainable aviation fuel production.”

The project will be led by Andy Billig, Co-President, Commercial and External Affairs, and Steve Drennan, Co-President and Project Director. Andy will focus on strategic partnerships and stakeholder engagement, while Steve will oversee development and technical delivery. They will work closely with SkyNRG’s wider leadership team, including Jessie van der Linden, VP of Projects, who will serve as a key SkyNRG counterpart supporting governance and delivery.

Together, SkyNRG, Technip Energies, Topsoe, Sasol and other project partners, including Boeing, are working to advance Project Wigeon toward commercial-scale SAF production and support the continued growth of advanced SAF supply in North America.

text:
Wood Based Biofuel Market Size

The Wood Based Biofuel Market was valued at USD 4.42 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 5.22 billion in 2026, expanding at a 16.1% CAGR (2026-2035) to USD 20.07 billion by 2035. Wood-based biofuels are advanced fuels and intermediates produced from lignocellulosic resources, including forest residues, industrial wood waste, plantation wood, and pulp-industry co-products.

The market is moving from isolated demonstration projects toward integrated biorefinery systems that connect forestry, pulp, refining, and fuel-distribution assets. Its commercial trajectory depends on whether developers can secure certified feedstock at predictable delivered costs while directing output into applications where drop-in performance, compliance value, and long-term offtake support premium pricing.

Wood Based Biofuel Market Trends, Growth Drivers & GMI Forecast Outlook

Aviation decarbonization policy is redirecting lignocellulosic conversion investment toward certified liquid fuels, while feedstock collection economics and process complexity continue to limit the speed at which new capacity can be commissioned. The resulting outlook favors scalable, financeable pathways with credible long-term offtake.

Key Drivers

*Evidence anchors use cited external data; demand implications and forecast conditions represent GMI analysis.*

ReFuelEU turns aviation fuel blending from a voluntary procurement initiative into a recurring compliance requirement. That change improves the bankability of projects able to document feedstock eligibility, chain-of-custody controls, and fuel quality. For wood-based suppliers, the commercial benefit is not merely additional demand: it is greater visibility into the timing and durability of airline and fuel-supplier offtake.

The rapid expansion of SAF output demonstrates that policy support, offtake agreements, and project execution can align at commercial scale. Wood-derived pathways remain differentiated by their potential to expand the feedstock pool beyond lipid-based materials, particularly where forest-industry residues and pulp co-products can be integrated into existing industrial sites.

ASTM-qualified Fischer-Tropsch and ATJ-SPK routes reduce buyer adoption friction because airlines, airports, and fuel handlers can use blended drop-in fuels within existing operating systems. This compatibility shifts diligence toward feedstock qualification, process reliability, and project economics, rather than requiring customers to commit to new aircraft or distribution infrastructure.

Key Restraints

*Evidence anchors use cited external data; demand implications and forecast conditions represent GMI analysis.*

The cost of collecting, sorting, drying, and transporting woody biomass creates a location-specific hurdle that cannot be resolved solely through conversion innovation. Projects must match plant scale with a defensible procurement radius, reliable seasonal availability, and feedstock specifications that preserve conversion yields. These constraints favor co-location with established forestry, sawmill, or pulp-industry infrastructure.

Cellulosic supply shortfalls indicate that policy demand alone does not guarantee deployable capacity. Developers must manage feedstock heterogeneity, pretreatment performance, enzyme economics, construction risk, and sustained plant availability before regulatory demand can translate into dependable fuel output.

Pretreatment remains a meaningful operational barrier because the composition and moisture profile of woody biomass affect both processing severity and downstream yield. Thermochemical projects face their own engineering challenges, but their ability to produce liquid hydrocarbon intermediates at large scale can be more readily aligned with aviation-fuel offtake structures.

Wood Based Biofuel Market Segment Analysis

By Fuel Type

Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Sustainable aviation fuel generated USD 1.86 billion in revenue in 2025 and is projected to account for 50.5% of Wood Based Biofuel Market revenue by 2035. SAF is becoming the principal value pool for advanced wood conversion because aviation has limited near-term alternatives to energy-dense liquid fuels. Developers with access to qualified woody feedstocks are therefore prioritizing pathways that can meet aviation specifications while supporting lender requirements for contracted demand.

Cellulosic Bioethanol

Cellulosic bioethanol held a 19.0% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 2.90 billion by 2035. The segment retains strategic importance in markets with ethanol-blending infrastructure and policy support for second-generation fuels. Its growth is nevertheless shaped by the operating consistency of pretreatment and fermentation systems, as well as competition for capital from projects targeting higher-value aviation markets.

Biomethanol

Biomethanol represented 14.4% of revenue in 2025 and is projected to expand at a 16.3% CAGR (2026-2035). Marine fuel demand and renewable chemical applications give biomethanol multiple outlets beyond road transport. Its commercial position strengthens where gasification capacity can be integrated with established methanol storage, handling, and customer networks.

Pyrolysis Oil

Pyrolysis oil generated USD 229.39 million in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 938.54 million by 2035. The segment's opportunity depends on advances in bio-oil stabilization, upgrading, and refinery co-processing. Its modular production profile may support regional deployment where residue availability is adequate but a large standalone gasification complex is not commercially justified.

Renewable Natural Gas

RNG held an 11.4% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 1.79 billion by 2035. Wood-derived RNG serves industrial heat, grid-adjacent uses, and selected heavy-duty transport demand. Its relative position is affected by the pace of vehicle electrification and by whether regional gas networks reward verified low-carbon molecules.

By Feedstock

Forest Residues & Logging Residues

Forest residues and logging residues generated USD 1.51 billion in 2025 and are expected to represent 30.6% of market revenue by 2035. This feedstock pool benefits from its connection to active timber harvesting, but project economics remain sensitive to collection density, terrain, moisture management, and sustainability requirements. Long-term supply agreements and local aggregation infrastructure are critical to converting theoretical resource availability into bankable feedstock.

Plantation Wood

Plantation wood held a 29.3% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 6.83 billion by 2035. Dedicated plantations offer greater control over quality, harvest scheduling, and traceability than dispersed residue streams. Their strategic value rises for large conversion facilities that need predictable biomass characteristics over multi-decade operating lives.

Pulp Mill Byproducts

Pulp mill byproducts generated USD 654.60 million in 2025 and are projected to grow at a 14.5% CAGR (2026-2035). Crude tall oil, black liquor, and lignin-rich streams benefit from industrial co-location and lower incremental collection requirements. Their value is amplified where existing pulp assets can provide consistent volumes, established logistics, and recognized sustainability documentation.

Sawmill Residues and Industrial Wood Waste

Sawmill residues and industrial wood waste held a 14.0% revenue share in 2025 and are projected to generate USD 3.04 billion by 2035. Sawdust, bark, chips, and off-specification wood can offer more concentrated supply than field-collected residues. The commercial challenge is managing heterogeneous material specifications while maintaining conversion performance and satisfying waste-stream qualification requirements.

By Conversion Technology

Biochemical Pathway

The biochemical pathway generated USD 1.27 billion in 2025 and is expected to account for 24.0% of market revenue by 2035. Biochemical conversion remains central to cellulosic ethanol production, particularly where policy and existing ethanol systems support deployment. Its competitive outlook depends on reducing variability in feedstock preparation and increasing plant reliability at industrial throughput.

Fischer-Tropsch

Fischer-Tropsch synthesis held a 28.2% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 6.60 billion by 2035. The pathway is increasingly favored for projects targeting liquid hydrocarbons across aviation and other difficult-to-electrify uses. Its appeal lies in the ability to transform syngas into flexible product streams, although gasification integration and capital intensity keep execution quality central to project viability.

Methanol Synthesis

Methanol synthesis represented 13.9% of revenue in 2025 and is forecast to grow at a 17.0% CAGR (2026-2035). The technology benefits from a mature global methanol-handling ecosystem and growing interest in renewable marine fuels and chemical feedstocks. Commercial success will depend on securing low-cost, dependable syngas while managing competition from other renewable methanol routes.

Fast Pyrolysis + Catalytic Upgrading

Fast pyrolysis plus catalytic upgrading held a 7.6% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 1.57 billion by 2035. This route can create an intermediate bio-oil close to dispersed biomass resources, then concentrate upgrading activity at refinery-linked sites. Catalyst performance, hydrogen access, and the stability of bio-oil during transport and storage remain decisive commercial variables.

Alcohol-to-Jet SPK

Alcohol-to-Jet SPK generated USD 947.15 million in 2025 and is expected to account for 20.4% of market revenue by 2035. ATJ-SPK provides a bridge between alcohol production and aviation-fuel demand. Its value proposition is strongest where cellulosic ethanol or biomethanol producers can access established aviation-fuel marketing channels and demonstrate reliable product qualification.

By Application

Aviation

Aviation generated USD 1.74 billion in 2025 and is projected to account for 46.7% of market revenue by 2035. Aviation is the most commercially compelling end market because fuel substitution is difficult, compliance obligations are strengthening, and buyers increasingly use long-term offtake to secure supply. This combination gives qualified SAF projects a clearer route to financing than many alternative wood-biofuel applications.

Road Transportation

Road transportation held a 17.7% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to grow at a 13.0% CAGR (2026-2035). The application remains material for heavy-duty and long-haul uses, but light-duty electrification limits the long-term strategic role of liquid biofuels. Producers are consequently assessing road fuel as a portfolio outlet rather than the sole anchor for capacity investment.

Marine Shipping

Marine shipping held a 10.1% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 2.19 billion by 2035. The adoption of methanol-capable vessels and more stringent maritime decarbonization objectives are opening a new route to market for wood-derived biomethanol. Demand development will depend on bunker availability, vessel ordering decisions, and shipping companies' willingness to contract for verified low-carbon fuel.

Industrial Chemicals and Bio-Based Materials

Industrial chemicals and bio-based materials generated USD 697.27 million in 2025 and are projected to reach USD 3.18 billion by 2035. Chemical applications can support attractive value realization because renewable intermediates may replace fossil-derived inputs in specialized products. Demand is less directly tied to vehicle-fleet turnover, although qualification cycles and customer specifications can lengthen commercialization timelines.

Power and Heat Generation

Power and heat generation held a 14.4% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to account for 10.8% of market revenue by 2035. Wood biomass is increasingly directed toward applications that can capture higher compliance and decarbonization value than conventional energy generation. Power and heat therefore remain important local outlets but face an opportunity-cost disadvantage where aviation, marine, or chemical demand is accessible.

Wood Based Biofuel Market Regional Analysis

The Wood Based Biofuel Market in North America generated USD 1.60 billion in 2025 and is projected to account for 33.7% of global revenue by 2035. The region combines established forest resources, advanced fuel-policy mechanisms, and an expanding project-development ecosystem. Investment outcomes will be shaped by regulatory continuity, the availability of tax incentives, and the ability of developers to translate resource availability into contracted, certifiable supply chains.

U.S.

The United States generated USD 1.17 billion in 2025 and is projected to hold 70.6% of North American revenue by 2035. Federal fuel obligations and clean-fuel incentives provide an important foundation for investment, but commercial deployment remains exposed to permitting, first-of-a-kind construction risk, and demonstrated plant performance. Wood-to-SAF development is gaining strategic relevance where developers can pair forestry resources with committed aviation demand.

Canada

Canada held an 18.3% North American revenue share in 2025 and is projected to expand at a 16.1% CAGR (2026-2035). Canada's certified forest base and clean-fuel framework provide favorable conditions for advanced biofuel development. The market's differentiator will be whether residue supplies can be aggregated at a scale and cost appropriate for industrial conversion facilities.

Mexico

Mexico held an 8.4% North American revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 661.65 million by 2035. Plantation resources and proximity to North American aviation markets create a potential advantage for Mexican developers. The primary need is greater maturity in feedstock logistics, project financing, and domestic mechanisms that support advanced-fuel offtake.

Europe Wood Based Biofuel Market Analysis

Europe held a 40.9% revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 8.46 billion by 2035. Europe's leadership reflects the intersection of mature forestry and pulp assets with increasingly prescriptive renewable-fuel policy. Its established residue supply chains, sustainability frameworks, and aviation demand signals make the region a focal point for commercial wood-to-liquid capacity.

Germany

Germany generated USD 288.94 million in 2025 and is expected to account for 17.0% of European revenue by 2035. Germany's opportunity is supported by industrial demand for renewable molecules, sophisticated logistics, and access to European compliance markets. Project economics will depend on securing feedstock competitively against other material and energy uses.

Austria held a 7.9% European revenue share in 2025 and is projected to generate USD 719.11 million by 2035. Austria's established biomass-energy base and forestry sector offer a platform for advanced-fuel expansion. Its proximity to Central European markets can support feedstock and product flows, particularly for projects with credible sustainability certification.

Its competitive position is reinforced where industrial co-products can be directed into higher-value fuel pathways without disrupting core pulp and timber economics.

Developers that combine domestic residues, port infrastructure, and durable offtake arrangements are best positioned to manage that tension.

Asia Pacific Wood Based Biofuel Market Analysis

The Wood Based Biofuel Market in Asia Pacific generated USD 653.27 million in 2025 and is projected to grow at a 17.6% CAGR (2026-2035). Asia Pacific combines rapidly developing biofuel policy with highly varied feedstock conditions and industrial capabilities. Market development will depend on the integration of forestry resources with reliable conversion capacity and fuel-distribution channels.

Wood Based Biofuel Market Share & Competitive Landscape

UPM

text:
India has achieved a 52% readiness score for sustainable aviation fuel as the country prepares to increase the use of cleaner fuels in aviation, according to an assessment by Boeing and the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials.

The findings, reported by Financial Express, come as India moves from developing its SAF ecosystem towards wider commercial adoption. The country has set a phased blending roadmap, targeting 1% SAF in 2027, 2% in 2028 and 5% by 2030.

At the 2030 target, annual SAF demand from domestic and international aviation is expected to reach around 720 million litres, or 0.6 million tonnes. By comparison, India's estimated SAF production potential stands at 14 million to 33 million tonnes a year.

Also Read | Layoffs Are Rising In Tech, But These Skills Are Helping People Unlock Better Pay

That gap highlights a key challenge for the sector. India may have significant production potential, but building the infrastructure and commercial network needed to use SAF at scale will require coordinated action across several areas.

Also Read | On-Time Flight Performance: Air India Ranks Third; Check OTP Of IndiGo, Akasa Air, SpiceJet

The Boeing-RSB assessment examined the country's preparedness across nine components, including feedstock availability, production capacity, regulations, logistics, market demand, financing, research and development, technology and supporting infrastructure.

The report stressed that higher production capacity alone will not be enough to accelerate adoption. Policy support, investment and financing, supply-chain development and technological capabilities will also need to expand alongside production.

India is also committed to joining the International Civil Aviation Organization's CORSIA programme from 2027, adding another policy dimension to its efforts to reduce aviation emissions.

Boeing India and South Asia President Salil Gupte said India's position as one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets gives the country an important role in sustainable aviation.

Also Read | India's Aviation Sector To Support 20 Million Jobs By 2040, Says Rammohan Naidu

RSB Executive Director Bettina Paschke said the assessment provides stakeholders with a common evidence base to guide further development of India's SAF ecosystem.

The assessment indicates that India has established several foundations for SAF adoption, but turning its production potential into actual aviation fuel use will depend on coordinated progress across policy, financing, infrastructure, technology and supply chains.

title: News Extra September 2026 - GreenAir News
description:
International Airlines Group (IAG) has selected OpenAirlines’ SkyBreathe fuel-efficiency platform to support more than 600 aircraft of its combined fleet.
The facility is designed to produce 50 million gallons (143 kt) of SAF annually using RNG and Fischer-Tropsch technology.
The 2026 theme is ‘Collective Momentum’, to reflect the focus on collaboration and the role of shared action in driving sustainability progress.
ARC-Bio, a JV between Bioénergie AECN and Alder Renewables, reports a successful demonstration of a pathway to produce SAF from Canadian forestry residues through refinery co-processing.
SAF technology provider Axens has signed a MoU with Hong Kong-based EPC services provider Wison Engineering to explore collaboration opportunities on global SAF and eSAF projects, including the Fischer-Tropsch pathway.
text:
Japan Airlines and Climeworks Solutions have announced what they describe as the world’s first purchase agreement for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) credits designed to meet the requirements of ICAO’s CORSIA carbon scheme. As one of the first airlines to retire large-scale CORSIA-eligible credits, JAL says its helping establish a new market and explore how high-integrity carbon removals, including technologies such as Direct Air Capture can complement aviation’s broader decarbonisation efforts, and will purchase Climeworks DAC credits as part of a wider CDR portfolio.

Aether Fuels reports it has successfully deployed its 2.5 barrel-per-day Aurora technology to produce ASTM-specification synthetic aviation fuel using renewable natural gas (RNG) and industrial CO2, which it says is a first for a North American company. Aether has a pipeline of commercial projects, including Project Beacon in Singapore that aims to produce 2,000 tonnes of SAF per year from industrial waste and biomethane. It has MoUs in place with Singapore Airlines, JetBlue and FlyORO.

International Airlines Group (IAG) has selected OpenAirlines’ SkyBreathe fuel-efficiency platform to support more than 600 aircraft of its combined fleet. The platform will provide a common data and reporting framework across IAG airlines Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL and Vueling, which will help them identify and monitor fuel-saving opportunities, measure performance and share successful initiatives.

SkyNRG has chosen Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe as key partners for the FEED phase of its Project Wigeon SAF facility in Washington State as it moves towards a future FID. The facility is designed to produce 50 million gallons (143 kt) of SAF annually using RNG and Fischer-Tropsch technology. Key permitting has been secured, says SkyNRG, and start-up is targeted for 2031. Meanwhile, Emerson has been awarded a contract by Technip to provide automation technologies for the SkyNRG DSL-01 SAF facility now under construction in the Netherlands.

The SkyTeam airline alliance has launched the fifth edition of The Aviation Challenge, which brings together airlines and industry stakeholders to develop, implement and scale solutions aimed at reducing aviation’s environmental impact. The 2026 theme is ‘Collective Momentum’, to reflect the focus on collaboration and the role of shared action in driving sustainability progress. Participants are to submit their entries by the beginning of November, with winners across 21 award categories announced in January 2027.

Norway’s NOEMI Aerospace, which is developing a fully electric amphibious aircraft for regional passenger transport, with the ability to operate from both water and conventional runways, has signed a MoU with SkyHop Aviation, India’s first dedicated commercial seaplane operators. The deal will see the introduction of up to 15 NOEMI aircraft into the Indian market. Entry into service for the aircraft is targeted for 2030.

Heart Aerospace has unveiled the ES-36, a 36-seat hybrid-electric regional airliner, which adds six more passenger seats and 1,415 pounds of payload capacity to the previously announced ES-30. The ES-36 also moves from four to two nacelles and propellers, which the company says will reduce the number of propulsion components to maintain, so lowering maintenance costs. First flight of the ES-36 is targeted for the second half of 2028 and entry into service in 2031. US charter air carrier JSX has announced a deposit-backed purchase agreement for 50 ES-36 aircraft, with purchase rights for 50 more.

ARC-Bio, a JV between Bioénergie AECN and Alder Renewables, reports a successful demonstration of a pathway to produce SAF from Canadian forestry residues through refinery co-processing. The project upgraded fast pyrolysis oil from forestry residues by Bioénergie AECN in Quebec into barrel-scale quantities of Alder Renewable Crude (ARC). This biocrude was then processed in a fluid catalytic cracking pilot unit that simulates commercial refinery operations at sites worldwide.

Singapore-based FlyORO Technologies has signed a Letter of Intent with ICAO to join the ICAO Finvest Hub, an initiative to connect aviation decarbonisation projects with sources of investment. FlyORO will contribute its operating experience in modular SAF blending solutions, the step at which certified neat SAF is combined with conventional jet fuel to produce a finished, specification-compliant product that can be uplifted into an aircraft.

France’s Haffner Energy has launched SB-HEFA (solid biomass to HEFA), a process for producing renewable diesel and SAF based on its proprietary thermolysis technology, which directly converts solid biomass into liquid without going through syngas. The company says SB-HEFA can provide a more direct, simpler and cost-effective route to SAF production than alternative technologies. It estimates the CAPEX of a SB-HEFA facility could be around a one-third that of a solid biomass to liquid fuels conversion chain based on Fischer-Tropsch or methanol synthesis.

SAF technology provider Axens has signed a MoU with Hong Kong-based EPC services provider Wison Engineering to explore collaboration opportunities on global SAF and eSAF projects, including the Fischer-Tropsch pathway. The objective, they say, is to develop eSAF solutions designed for greater cost and schedule predictability, rapid deployment and efficient replication across global markets. Axens has also been selected by Canadian SAF producer Expander Energy to provide its advanced FT Liquid Upgrading technology at two developments in Alberta and British Columbia.

The Polish Association for Decarbonisation of Aviation (PSDL) has published a report that assesses the actual carbon footprint of the Polish aviation sector, provide forecasts through to 2032 and create a shared reference point for discussions on decarbonisation. The report shows that passenger numbers will rise from 66.1 million in 2025 to almost 86 million in 2032. CO2 emissions related to passenger traffic will increase from 5.01 million tonnes to around 5.2 million tonnes. Emissions per passenger are expected to fall by 4.5% due to fleet renewal, the increasing use of SAF and operational efficiency improvements.

The German press agency, dpa, reports the Federal Ministry of Transport is to impose penalties of €1,332 ($1,500) per tonne of SAF that airlines fail to use as required by the EU’s ReFuelEU SAF mandate. Applicable from the start of 2025, the mandate requires a 2% minimum blend of SAF be available at EU airports, then rising to 6%, with a separate 1.2% eSAF requirement, in 2030.

text:
RESEARCH TRIANGLE PARK, N.C. and CHICAGO, Sept. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aether Fuels Inc. (Aether), a sustainable fuels technology company, announced the successful construction, commissioning, and operation of its fully integrated demonstration line, including the production of synthetic aviation fuel which meets the specifications of ASTM D7566, the international standard for synthetic jet fuel. This is a major milestone in the commercialization of its Aether Aurora™ technology platform.

This demonstration line utilized Aether’s 2.5 barrel-per-day capacity Aether Aurora Tri-Converter and Aurora Upgrader units, integrated together with RTI’s existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor. The fuel was produced using mass-balanced renewable natural gas (RNG) derived from landfill gas generated in Kentucky and industrial CO2 as feedstocks and included the complete conversion process from waste-derived gas feedstocks to fully upgraded synthetic liquid jet fuel. Aether is believed to be the first company in North America to produce ASTM-specification synthetic aviation fuel from mass-balanced RNG and captured industrial CO2 at this scale.

Independent third-party testing conducted by AmSpec (www.amspecgroup.com) confirmed that the fuel samples produced during this demo run met the applicable ASTM specifications for FT-SPK (Annex A1 for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK)). Under the ASTM D7566 standard, alternative fuels meeting this specification are approved for blending with conventional kerosene up to 50% without requiring modifications to existing aircraft tanks, pipelines, or airport fueling systems. Additionally, because the FT-SPK route is already approved under the ASTM, no new ASTM certification is required.

“This demonstration proves Aether’s ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel. It is the culmination of over a year of hard work by Aether’s R&D team and is a tremendous milestone,” said Dhaval Shah, Chief Technology Officer of Aether Fuels. “Just as importantly, the data from this demonstration informs and de-risks the design of our 50 BPD Project Beacon plant in Singapore, as we continue rapid journey to large scale commercial deployment”

Building Toward Commercial Deployment

The demonstration builds on Aether’s previously reported stand-alone demonstration of the Tri-Converter unit with GTI Energy and represents the latest step in Aether’s progression from the lab to commercial deployment, and represents important technical validation ahead of Project Beacon, Aether’s planned 2,000 metric tons per year (50 barrels per day) commercial project in Singapore.

Aether has a pipeline of large commercial projects under development that will follow Project Beacon and produce ASTM D7566-compliant sustainable aviation fuel with lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions of over 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.

“This is exciting progress for Aether as we march forward towards commercial deployment,” said Conor Madigan, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Aether Fuels. “We started by systematically demonstrating each part of the Aurora platform at the pilot scale, then scaled our novel technology up more than 50X in standalone demo units, and in this most recent demonstration, brought these demo units together in an integrated line that produces ASTM spec jet fuel. This is a significant achievement and puts us on the right track to successfully build and operate Project Beacon and the commercial projects that will follow.”

Aether Fuels is a climate technology company revolutionizing sustainable fuel production to help hard-to-abate industries like aviation and ocean shipping achieve their decarbonization goals. Our breakthrough Aether Aurora™ technology converts waste carbon into drop-in liquid fuels with near-ideal carbon conversion efficiency. title: Rising SAF production costs sharpen focus on blending and supply logistics - Fastmarkets
description:
From production cost to delivered cost For SAF producers and suppliers, however, the economics do not stop when the fuel leaves the refinery.
SAF is produced as a synthetic blending component that must be blended with conventional aviation fuel before it can be used as finished jet fuel.
“Rather than transporting a bulk of blended SAF, when the airport already has Jet A-1 onsite, blending last-mile allows the airport to simply truck in neat SAF volumes instead,” Toh told Fastmarkets.

text:
Fastmarkets’ cost-based assessments show that SAF production economics have become more challenging since the first half of 2026.

The sustainable aviation fuel (SAF max), base cost, exw Netherlands assessment rose to $2,430 per tonne on September 18 from a 2026 low of $1,902 per tonne on March 13, up by around 28%. The sustainable aviation fuel (HVO max), base cost, exw Netherlands assessment rose to $2,553 per tonne on September 18 from a 2026 low of $1,922 per tonne on March 13, up by around 33%.

Feedstock has been a significant driver of that increase, though not the only one.

Fastmarkets’ daily China bulk used cooking oil (UCO) assessment rose to $1,182 per tonne on September 18 from $1,020 per tonne on March 13, up by around 16%, while the weekly crude palm oil mill effluent (POME), fob Malaysia price rose to $1,170 per tonne on September 17 from $1,090 per tonne on March 12, up by around 7%.

Both increases are more modest than the roughly 28% rise in the SAF production-cost assessment and 33% rise in the HVO production-cost assessment over the period, indicating that factors beyond feedstock, including hydrogen costs and changes in co-product values, have also influenced production economics.

UCO remains the largest single cost component in hydrotreated esters and fatty acids (HEFA) production economics, meaning changes in feedstock values can have a significant impact on the cost of producing SAF, alongside hydrogen costs and by-product values.

From production cost to delivered cost

For SAF producers and suppliers, however, the economics do not stop when the fuel leaves the refinery.

SAF is produced as a synthetic blending component that must be blended with conventional aviation fuel before it can be used as finished jet fuel. Once blended and certified, it can use existing aviation fuel infrastructure.

This creates a further supply-chain consideration: whether it is more efficient to transport a finished SAF blend or move the neat SAF component to a location where conventional Jet A-1 is already available.

According to Genevieve Toh, chief marketing officer at FlyORO, the distinction can be significant when fuel has to be transported to an airport by road.

“At a 10% blend, nine of every ten liters moved is conventional jet fuel already available at the destination, and it carries the same freight, storage and handling cost as the SAF fraction,” Toh told Fastmarkets.

If blending instead takes place at or close to the airport, only the 10,000 liters of neat SAF needs to be transported, while the conventional Jet A-1 can be sourced locally.

“The key difference is access,” Toh said, adding that strategically located blend points can extend SAF supply to regional and remote airports that may not be reached economically through existing centralized supply chains.

The potential benefit depends on the airport’s existing fuel infrastructure, the distance to supply hubs, the availability of storage and the cost and mode of transport. It does not reduce the underlying cost of producing the SAF, but it can change the downstream logistics required to deliver it.

The model is already being deployed at Toowoomba Wellcamp Airport in Australia, Toh said, where neat SAF is delivered to the site and blended with existing Jet A-1 rather than arriving as a finished blend through a separate supply chain.

Wellcamp Airport is further inland than many of Australia’s larger airports and does not have pipelines directly connecting it with ports or fuel terminals. Jet fuel therefore has to be transported to the airport by truck, including SAF.

“Rather than transporting a bulk of blended SAF, when the airport already has Jet A-1 onsite, blending last-mile allows the airport to simply truck in neat SAF volumes instead,” Toh told Fastmarkets.

The entire facility is designed to handle 100,000 liters of blended SAF. At a 30% blend ratio, for example, the airport would need to truck in 30,000 liters of neat SAF and blend it onsite, rather than transporting 100,000 liters of finished blended SAF.

“This reduces the delivered cost of transporting bulk volumes and the associated transport emissions too,” Toh said.

The source of the neat SAF supplied to Wellcamp is confidential, Toh said, but the fuel is trucked into the airport.

The example illustrates why the location of the blend point can become a relevant part of SAF supply economics, particularly for airports that already have conventional jet fuel infrastructure but lack direct connections to SAF production or major fuel terminals. In such cases, moving the SAF component separately can avoid transporting conventional jet fuel that is already available at the destination.

The economics will vary by airport, supply route, blend ratio, available tankage and freight mode. The key question is therefore not simply where SAF is produced, but how the SAF component moves from the production site to the point where it is ultimately uplifted.

Where the feedstock is actually moving

As feedstock costs rise, where the tonnes physically move matters more, not less.

China’s export data underscores how concentrated, and how quickly shifting, that geography is. Fastmarkets’ tracking of Chinese General Administration of Customs (GACC) data shows UCO exports reached around 2.3 million tonnes in the first seven months of 2026, up by roughly 60% on the same period in 2025.

The Netherlands and the United States remained the two largest destinations, together accounting for around 40% of the total and each up by more than 60% year on year, consistent with the Netherlands assessment above being based on Rotterdam-area supply.

Singapore moved the other way – Chinese UCO volumes to Singapore fell by around 22% over the same period even as total exports surged, while volumes to Malaysia more than doubled.

The shift points to feedstock consolidating around Europe’s processing hub even as Asia’s own blending debate continues.

Testing whether it’s infrastructure, or feedstock, holding regional airports back

Malaysia’s own trade data offers a way to test Toh’s “access” argument directly. Intertek Testing Services (ITS) export data covering Malaysia’s UCO and other feedstocks shows total exports of just over 1.5 million tonnes in the first eight months of 2026.

According to ITS, Neste was by far the largest buyer, accounting for around 42% of that volume, and its purchases split almost evenly between two destinations: Rotterdam, at roughly 50%, and Singapore’s plant, at roughly 45%. Between them, the Netherlands and Singapore accounted for more than half of all Malaysian export volumes across these products.

That pattern supports Toh’s framing: regional airport access looks to be constrained more by where processing infrastructure already sits than by feedstock availability.

Malaysia produces substantial volumes of POME and UCO, but almost all of the tracked material leaves the country for one of two centralized hubs rather than being converted domestically, and a large share of it is bound for the same Tuas refinery at the center of Singapore’s own SAF supply chain.

A live precedent in Singapore

That Tuas connection points to a working example of the model Aether Fuels and other companies have proposed for Bukom Island. At its Tuas refinery, Neste produces neat SAF before it is sent to a blending facility to be combined with conventional fuel and certified to meet jet fuel standards, before final delivery to airlines at Changi Airport.

The refinery’s expansion took Neste’s Singapore capacity to 2.6 million tonnes annually, of which up to one million tonnes can be SAF.

The comparison is a useful one: the same conceptual model – neat SAF produced at one site, blended at another, delivered to Changi – is already operating at refinery scale in Singapore, drawing on Malaysian feedstock among other sources, ahead of newer decentralized proposals targeting locations without an existing on-site refinery.

Where the same question could apply next

China’s own SAF pathway suggests where the blending-location question could apply next, though the timeline is less advanced than in Singapore. A pilot program launched by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) in September 2024 remains centered on the same four airports it started with – Beijing Daxing, Chengdu Shuangliu, Zhengzhou Xinzheng and Ningbo Lishe – where domestic flights have blended in 1% SAF since March 2025.

Separately, individual producers have begun extending real SAF refueling to other airports on a commercial rather than mandated basis: Eagros, for example, has run SAF-blended flights at Chengdu Shuangliu with China National Aviation Fuel Group (CNAF) since March 2026, and more recently extended that model to SF Airlines’ cargo hub at Ezhou Huahu.

China’s 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025) had set a 50,000-tonne cumulative SAF consumption target, but that plan period has now ended. Its successor, the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), approved in March 2026, places a stronger policy emphasis on low-carbon and green industry, but has not confirmed a specific SAF blending mandate.

In the meantime, China’s SAF industry has kept growing regardless: the country’s six export-licensed producers hold a combined export capacity of around 1.7 million tonnes a year, and exports have been climbing, with a record 101,000 tonnes shipped in May 2026 alone.

For now, that suggests commercial pull from export markets is running ahead of domestic, mandate-driven demand. If a domestic blending obligation does eventually land in the 15th Five-Year Plan period, though, China’s much larger and more dispersed airport network would face the same blending-location question that CyRee and Aether Fuels are currently addressing in Singapore.

text:
The assessment, released on Tuesday, provides a roadmap for India’s next phase of SAF development as the country moves from early-stage development towards wider adoption.

India has set SAF blending targets of 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030. The country is also committed to participating in the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) from 2027.

Under a 5% blending scenario in 2030, SAF demand across domestic and international aviation is projected at around 720 million litres, or about 0.6 million tonnes a year. This compares with an estimated production potential of 14-33 million tonnes annually.

The assessment evaluates India’s preparedness across nine areas, including feedstock, production capacity, policy and regulation, supply chains and logistics, market demand, investment and financing, research and development, technology readiness, and enabling infrastructure and services. It, however, points to the need for development of a wider ecosystem around SAF, with production potential alone not being sufficient to support adoption.

“As one of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets, India has an important role in enabling sustainable aviation – and pursuing a deliberate and well-researched path to SAF adoption is key,” said Salil Gupte, president, Boeing India & South Asia.

“This report is valuable because it confirms exactly where India has the foundational capacity to enable SAF adoption and because it identifies specific opportunities ahead,” Gupte added.

India’s SAF opportunity will depend on coordinated development across the broader ecosystem, including government policy, industry participation, financing, technology and infrastructure, the assessment said.

“India’s Sustainable Aviation Fuel opportunity is substantial. This assessment gives stakeholders a common evidence base from which to act, and RSB looks forward to continuing to convene and support the collaboration needed to translate India’s potential into sustainable impact,” said Bettina Paschke, executive director, RSB.

Boeing said it is committed to supporting airline customers and policymakers in India and globally in achieving emissions reduction goals by helping build a robust SAF ecosystem.
