Buying the certificate would not mean that a specific building, vehicle, turbine or other product was physically manufactured from the corresponding low-emissions steel.
RMI’s framework is intended to keep the contractual environmental claim separate from claims about the material actually contained in a product.
Credible Accounting Will Make or Break Steel Book and Claim
text:
Steel decarbonization is running into a problem that better production technology alone cannot fix: the companies prepared to support lower-emissions steel are not always located near the plants producing it.

In many cases, they are not even direct steel buyers.

RMI’s Steel Book and Claim Framework is designed to address that disconnect. The model would allow companies to purchase the verified environmental attributes associated with qualifying low-emissions iron or steel production without receiving the physical metal itself.

For steelmakers, that could create an additional revenue stream to support capital-intensive decarbonization projects. For companies with significant steel-related Scope 3 emissions, it offers a way to support cleaner production even when steel is buried several tiers deep in their supply chains.

The stakes are significant. RMI estimates that iron and steel account for roughly 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions, although estimates vary according to the accounting boundaries used. The International Energy Agency, for example, has estimated the sector represents about 7% of energy-system CO2 emissions.

Separating Low-Emissions Steel From the Environmental Attribute

Book and claim applies an approach already used in markets such as renewable electricity and sustainable aviation fuel: the physical product and its environmental benefit do not have to travel to the same customer.

Under RMI’s proposed system, qualifying production of low-emissions iron or steel generates an environmental attribute certificate. Once registered, the certificate becomes a book-and-claim unit, or BCU, corresponding to one metric ton of verified iron or steel.

The physical steel can continue through existing distribution channels. The BCU, meanwhile, can be purchased separately by a company seeking to support lower-emissions steelmaking.

Take a U.S. business whose steel arrives through fabricators, distributors or equipment suppliers. A European steelmaker may be producing substantially lower-emissions material, but restructuring the buyer’s entire supply chain to source from that facility could be commercially or logistically unrealistic.

Book and claim creates another route. The U.S. company could purchase and retire the environmental attributes generated by the European facility while the physical steel is sold elsewhere.

That distinction matters for corporate claims. Buying the certificate would not mean that a specific building, vehicle, turbine or other product was physically manufactured from the corresponding low-emissions steel. RMI’s framework is intended to keep the contractual environmental claim separate from claims about the material actually contained in a product.

RMI is also attempting to prevent the system from rewarding minor emissions reductions as though they represented deep decarbonization.

Eligibility is linked to emissions-intensity thresholds, with separate pathways for iron and crude steel. The methodology accounts for scrap content when setting steel thresholds and includes a Near-Zero Aligned designation for qualifying production at the lowest emissions levels.

The framework also sets conditions around production routes involving technologies such as fossil-fuel-based direct-reduced iron, carbon capture and biomass. The goal is to distinguish between different decarbonization pathways rather than treating every reduction in emissions intensity as interchangeable.

For producers, the commercial logic is significant. Hydrogen-based direct-reduced iron, electrification and other low-emissions production routes can require substantial capital investment before a large physical market exists for the resulting steel.

Book and claim potentially expands that market. Producers would no longer depend exclusively on customers able and willing to take delivery from a particular facility. Buyers in other markets could contribute financially to the emissions improvement.

The approach could be particularly relevant for companies that influence steel demand without directly purchasing large volumes from mills.

Automakers can often engage directly with steel producers, while building owners, technology companies, renewable energy developers and other businesses may encounter steel primarily through construction contractors, machinery or manufactured components.

That leaves them with limited leverage over the original producer despite carrying steel-related emissions in their value chains. A book-and-claim system could allow those companies to aggregate demand across projects and geographies without first rebuilding established procurement networks.

In that sense, certificates are less about replacing physical procurement of lower-emissions steel and more about addressing a market-development gap. Early projects need customers prepared to pay a premium for reduced emissions. Requiring every one of those customers to physically receive the associated steel can sharply limit the available pool of capital.

text:
SkyNRG has selected Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe as key partners for the initial engineering activities of the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) phase of Project Wigeon, its planned sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility at the Port of Walla Walla in Washington State (U.S.).

The appointments bring together technology and engineering expertise to support Project Wigeon as it progresses into FEED, a key phase in further developing the project’s engineering, cost and execution plans towards a future Final Investment Decision (FID). Project Wigeon is designed to produce 50 million gallons (143 kt) of SAF annually using renewable natural gas (RNG) and commercially proven Fischer-Tropsch technology. With key permitting secured and start-up targeted for 2031, the project aims to add significant new SAF production capacity in North America.

Topsoe and Sasol have each signed a Basic Engineering Design Package agreement with SkyNRG, providing technology licenses, engineering design and technical services for their respective technologies. Project Wigeon will combine Topsoe’s SynCOR™ and hydroprocessing technologies with Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch technology to convert RNG into SAF.

Technip Energies brings extensive experience working with both Topsoe’s and Sasol’s technologies, alongside strong modularization capabilities to support the project’s execution. The appointment also builds on SkyNRG’s established relationship with Technip Energies through DSL-01, SkyNRG’s SAF production facility currently under construction in Delfzijl, the Netherlands.

Steve Drennan, Co-President and Project Director: “Bringing Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe on board is an important step in progressing Project Wigeon toward FEED. Together, we are combining proven technologies with deep engineering and project execution expertise to further develop a permitted, design-ready project and lay the foundations for commercial-scale advanced SAF production in the US.”

Loïc Chapuis, President Project Delivery and Services at Technip Energies, commented: “Project Wigeon marks a new step in our collaboration with SkyNRG, building on the work already underway on DSL-01 project in the Netherlands. This new milestone demonstrates how our engineering and project delivery expertise can support SkyNRG as it develops SAF projects across different geographies and contributes to the growth of sustainable aviation fuel production.”

The project will be led by Andy Billig, Co-President, Commercial and External Affairs, and Steve Drennan, Co-President and Project Director. Andy will focus on strategic partnerships and stakeholder engagement, while Steve will oversee development and technical delivery. They will work closely with SkyNRG’s wider leadership team, including Jessie van der Linden, VP of Projects, who will serve as a key SkyNRG counterpart supporting governance and delivery.

Together, SkyNRG, Technip Energies, Topsoe, Sasol and other project partners, including Boeing, are working to advance Project Wigeon toward commercial-scale SAF production and support the continued growth of advanced SAF supply in North America.

title: Canada's Investment Boom Must Reach Beyond Big Cities, Says Rural Prosperity Group
description:
Advocating for Rural Canada The Rural Prosperity Group is a Canadian advocacy organization focused on ensuring government decision-makers prioritize and protect rural communities.
The organization also encourages governments to review existing policies to ensure they support, rather than hinder, rural economic growth.
Growth Requires Infrastructure The Rural Prosperity Group and other rural advocates contend that investment discussions must also recognize the infrastructure required to support development.
A Rural Lens for Economic Growth The Rural Prosperity Group argues that applying a rural lens to policy decisions could help address some of these challenges.
The Rural Prosperity Group's message is that rural communities should not be viewed simply as locations where resources happen to exist.
text:
With billions flowing toward agriculture, critical minerals and processing projects, rural advocates say local communities must share in both the benefits and decision-making.

Canada’s first-ever Investment Summit generated headlines for the sheer size of the commitments announced.

Federal officials said the event attracted investment commitments approaching $500 billion, with projects spanning critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, infrastructure and agriculture. For policymakers, the summit marked an opportunity to showcase Canada as a destination for long-term capital investment and economic growth.

For many rural leaders, however, the conversation does not end with how much money is pledged.

The more important question may be whether rural and northern communities will have a meaningful role in helping shape, support and benefit from the projects that emerge from these investments.

That is a topic the Rural Prosperity Group believes deserves greater attention.

Advocating for Rural Canada

The Rural Prosperity Group is a Canadian advocacy organization focused on ensuring government decision-makers prioritize and protect rural communities. The group promotes the use of a "rural lens" when developing federal policies, programs and regulations, arguing that governments should consider how decisions made in Ottawa affect communities outside major urban centres.

The organization also encourages governments to review existing policies to ensure they support, rather than hinder, rural economic growth.

That perspective has become increasingly relevant as governments and investors focus on sectors such as critical minerals, food production, agri-food processing and renewable energy, industries that depend heavily on rural and northern Canada.

While investment announcements often focus on national economic benefits, many of the projects themselves are located in smaller communities that supply the land, workforce, transportation corridors and natural resources needed to make those developments possible.

Agriculture Featured Prominently

Agriculture and value-added processing were among the sectors highlighted during the summit.

Several provinces promoted projects designed to strengthen domestic processing capacity and create new opportunities for rural economies.

Manitoba highlighted a greenhouse expansion, a proposed soybean crushing facility and a sustainable aviation fuel initiative. Ontario promoted the Martison Phosphate Project near Hearst, which could play a role in fertilizer production as well as industrial and battery-mineral supply chains. Other provinces emphasized agriculture, agri-food manufacturing and value-added processing opportunities.

For farmers, these projects represent more than investment figures.

A soybean crop processed within Canada can support local employment, strengthen domestic supply chains and create additional demand for agricultural production. Fertilizer and processing facilities can generate economic activity well beyond the farm gate while helping Canada capture more value from commodities before they leave the country.

Many rural advocates argue that such projects demonstrate how economic growth can be created when Canada moves beyond producing raw commodities and focuses on processing and manufacturing closer to where resources are produced.

Growth Requires Infrastructure

The Rural Prosperity Group and other rural advocates contend that investment discussions must also recognize the infrastructure required to support development.

New processing facilities require reliable electricity, transportation networks, water access and skilled workers. Expanding industries can increase pressure on housing, roads, healthcare services and municipal infrastructure.

These challenges are often felt most directly by local governments and residents.

The issue extends beyond agriculture. Communities involved in mining, forestry, energy development and manufacturing frequently carry the responsibility of maintaining the infrastructure that supports industrial growth.

Advocates note that while economic benefits from major projects may be distributed nationally, many of the costs associated with growth are experienced locally.

Without sufficient planning and support, communities may struggle to accommodate new investment opportunities even when they welcome economic development.

A Rural Lens for Economic Growth

The Rural Prosperity Group argues that applying a rural lens to policy decisions could help address some of these challenges.

The concept calls on governments to evaluate how new regulations, programs and funding decisions affect rural communities before they are implemented. Supporters believe this approach could help ensure infrastructure, housing, transportation and workforce needs are considered alongside investment attraction efforts.

For agriculture, the approach may be particularly important.

Canada's farms, food processors and agricultural supply chains are concentrated in rural communities. As governments pursue growth in sectors such as food manufacturing, renewable fuels and fertilizer production, the success of those investments will depend in part on the strength and resilience of the communities that host them.

Looking Beyond the Announcement Stage

The Canada Investment Summit succeeded in drawing attention from investors and highlighting Canada's economic potential.

However, the long-term impact will depend on what projects ultimately move forward and how benefits are shared across the country.

For rural Canada, success will not be measured solely by the number of investment announcements or the size of capital commitments. It will also depend on whether communities have the infrastructure, workforce and resources needed to support sustainable growth.

The Rural Prosperity Group's message is that rural communities should not be viewed simply as locations where resources happen to exist. They are essential partners in Canada's economy and play a critical role in food production, manufacturing, processing and resource development.

As Canada pursues ambitious economic growth goals, the organization argues that ensuring rural and northern communities share in both the opportunities and decision-making process will be essential.

The investment story may begin in government offices and corporate boardrooms, but its success will ultimately be determined in rural municipalities, farming regions, processing facilities and small communities across the country.

That is where many of Canada's most important economic assets are located, and where the next chapter of growth may ultimately be written.

title: Germany, Austria and Luxembourg Launch €2.12 Billion eSAF Support Scheme
description:
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have launched a joint funding initiative worth up to €2.12 billion to accelerate the development and market uptake of electricity-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel (eSAF) in Europe.
Double-Sided Auction Targets Investment Gap The funding mechanism addresses a structural challenge facing emerging eSAF production.
Producers typically require long-term offtake commitments to secure financing for new facilities, while airlines and other fuel buyers generally purchase aviation fuel under shorter-term contracts.
Under the mechanism, eSAF producers will submit offers while prospective buyers submit their demand through a competitive process.
The coalition was established to encourage cooperation, exchange experience and mobilise financial support for synthetic aviation fuel production across Europe.
text:
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have launched a joint funding initiative worth up to €2.12 billion to accelerate the development and market uptake of electricity-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel (eSAF) in Europe.

Under the programme, Germany will provide up to €2 billion, while Austria and Luxembourg will each contribute up to €60 million. The initiative will use a double-sided auction mechanism designed to bring eSAF producers and buyers together while using public funding to help bridge gaps between supply and demand prices.

The three countries said the objective is to create stronger investment conditions for new eSAF production facilities while developing a competitive market for purchasing the fuel.

Double-Sided Auction Targets Investment Gap

The funding mechanism addresses a structural challenge facing emerging eSAF production.

Producers typically require long-term offtake commitments to secure financing for new facilities, while airlines and other fuel buyers generally purchase aviation fuel under shorter-term contracts. This difference in investment horizons can make it difficult for developers to secure final investment decisions for large-scale production projects.

The proposed double-sided auction is designed to address that gap.

Under the mechanism, eSAF producers will submit offers while prospective buyers submit their demand through a competitive process. An intermediary will then use government support to bridge any remaining difference between the supply and demand prices.

The governments said the approach is intended to combine long-term revenue visibility for producers with competitive purchasing conditions for buyers.

Funding Linked to National Contributions

The supported eSAF volumes will be placed on the markets of Germany, Austria and Luxembourg in proportion to each country’s contribution to the programme.

Germany’s contribution represents the largest share of the funding, while Austria and Luxembourg will each provide up to €60 million.

The programme is intended to support investment in new production capacity and establish a more developed European market for synthetic aviation fuel.

Germany’s Federal Ministry of Transport said its national market consultation on the planned funding mechanism had been completed, with feedback from industry and academia indicating broad interest in accelerating eSAF production and addressing existing investment barriers.

Programme Requires EU State-Aid Approval

The joint funding scheme is subject to approval under European Union state-aid rules by the European Commission.

The requirement means that the announcement establishes the framework for the programme and its intended funding commitments, but implementation remains dependent on the relevant regulatory approval.

The European Commission has already identified double-sided auctions as a potential mechanism for reducing investment and revenue risks associated with renewable aviation fuels.

The Commission’s eSAF Early Movers Coalition, launched in December 2025, brings together EU member states seeking to accelerate production and uptake of synthetic aviation fuels. Members agreed to cooperate on double-sided auctions, with an initial auction planned for 2026.

eSAF at the Centre of European Aviation Decarbonisation

Electricity-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel, also referred to as power-to-liquid fuel, is produced using renewable hydrogen and sustainable carbon. The hydrogen is generated through electrolysis using renewable electricity.

The European Commission considers eSAF an important component of the aviation sector’s transition towards lower-carbon fuels. Under the ReFuelEU Aviation framework, eSAF is required to account for 1.2% of fuel supplied at EU airports by 2030, increasing to 35% by 2050.

The Commission has also identified a significant need for new investment in renewable and low-carbon fuel production. Its Sustainable Transport Investment Plan estimates that more than €100 billion of investment will be needed by 2035 to scale up production of renewable and low-carbon fuels across transport.

Three Founding Coalition Members

Germany, Austria and Luxembourg are founding members of the eSAF Early Movers Coalition, which was launched in December 2025 alongside Finland, France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain.

The coalition was established to encourage cooperation, exchange experience and mobilise financial support for synthetic aviation fuel production across Europe.

The new three-country funding programme represents the next stage of that cooperation, with the participating governments seeking to move from policy commitments towards mechanisms capable of supporting actual production investments.

For airlines and the wider aviation fuel supply chain, increased eSAF production could provide an additional source of lower-carbon fuel while helping Europe develop domestic production capacity and reduce dependence on imported aviation fuels.

The programme therefore combines climate, industrial and energy-security objectives, with its eventual impact depending on the outcome of the state-aid approval process and the ability of the auction mechanism to unlock investment in commercial-scale eSAF production.

title: Higher Fuel Costs Not Curbing Alaska Air Group's International Ambitions - Leeham News
description:
With longer flight stages comes greater fuel costs—on top of what is already the U.S. airline sector's heaviest fuel-cost burden at baseline.
But the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines and Horizon Air has no intentions of curbing its growth plan, according to Jason Berry, Alaska's chief operating officer.
He addressed still-elevated fuel prices at the Aerospace Futures Alliance's annual conference in Seattle on September 24.
Asked by Leeham News and Analysis (LNA) whether Alaska Air Group has been forced to adjust its long-haul expansion or consider earlier-than-expected aircraft retirements, Berry said that rising fuel costs "are a real thing and it's a challenge."
In the shorter term, higher fuel costs are one of the scenarios the company's management team plans for.
text:
By Howard Hardee • Editor

September 28, 2026

Subscription Required

The trickle of oil escaping from the Strait of Hormuz and associated surge in jet fuel prices are unwelcome developments for all global airlines but come at an especially critical time for Alaska Air Group.

The airline company is in an early phase of an ambitious expansion plan, as it adds a host of international destinations and continues taking Boeing 787 Dreamliners to build a long-haul network out of Seattle. With longer flight stages comes greater fuel costs—on top of what is already the U.S. airline sector's heaviest fuel-cost burden at baseline.

But the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines and Horizon Air has no intentions of curbing its growth plan, according to Jason Berry, Alaska's chief operating officer. He addressed still-elevated fuel prices at the Aerospace Futures Alliance's annual conference in Seattle on September 24.

Asked by Leeham News and Analysis (LNA) whether Alaska Air Group has been forced to adjust its long-haul expansion or consider earlier-than-expected aircraft retirements, Berry said that rising fuel costs "are a real thing and it's a challenge."

"It's not just about this up-and-down of the volatility of the prices today," he said. "We all pay that equally, but we also have a disadvantage here on the West Coast, where our fuel prices are typically much more expensive that where our competitors get their fuel from the Gulf and the East Coast. So, we're working hard and diligently to find other ways to build resiliency into our fuel supply—not just from the current market, but for long term."

Notably, Berry suggested that exploring alternative fuels, such as sustainable aviation fuel, becomes more urgent in a high fuel cost environment. In the shorter term, higher fuel costs are one of the scenarios the company's management team plans for.

"We have a chicken and egg scenario here," he said. "We could slow down and scale back, but we know we have huge growth ambitions, and we need to continue to carry forward. We'll make some decisions on the fringes and on the edges where there's opportunities. But the reality is that we need to grow. Growth is critical to our future and we're going to continue to do that wisely."

text:
A new AASHTO report details the economic and community impact of general aviation in all 50 states, updating state-level figures for employment, payroll, economic output, airports, pilots and aircraft.

National Impact

The report estimates GA supports 1.33 million jobs nationwide, generates $107.5 billion in labor income and produces $339.2 billion in economic output. It places GA’s contribution to U.S. gross domestic product at $178.1 billion. Those national numbers come from a 2025 PricewaterhouseCoopers economic study based on 2023 data.

More than 4,400 public-use airports are accessible to general aviation, according to the report, compared with 549 airports served by scheduled commercial airlines. The state profiles also examine airport roles in business travel, agriculture, health care, emergency response, flight training and disaster relief. Recent airport investment has included projects such as $18.9 million in Kansas funding announced earlier this year for 53 airport projects.

State and Local Data

“For thousands of communities, general aviation airports are an essential part of the broader transportation system, connecting people and businesses to jobs, markets, health care, emergency services, and destinations across the country,” Alliance for Aviation Across America Executive Director Devin Osting said in the AASHTO announcement. “This report gives state and local transportation leaders the data and examples they need to show how those airports contribute to a prosperous economy and a connected, resilient national transportation network.”

The 68-page fourth edition updates the previous 2023 report using the latest available state aviation economic-impact studies and other government and industry data. It also includes sections examining advanced air mobility, uncrewed aircraft systems, alternative-powered aircraft and sustainable aviation fuel programs in several states.

The fourth edition of The Impact of General Aviation on State and Local Economies was produced by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials, the Alliance for Aviation Across America and the National Association of State Aviation Officials.

Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have opened a $2.5 billion funding mechanism aimed at accelerating Europe’s market for electricity-based sustainable aviation fuel.

text:
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have launched a joint $2.5 billion funding mechanism to narrow the price gap between e-SAF producers and buyers.

Around 50 synthetic aviation fuel projects across the EU are awaiting final investment decisions, according to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency.

The double-auction model aims to give producers long-term revenue certainty while allowing airlines and fuel buyers to maintain shorter procurement cycles.

Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have opened a $2.5 billion funding mechanism aimed at accelerating Europe’s market for electricity-based sustainable aviation fuel.

The programme is the first concrete project under the eSAF Early Movers’ Coalition, established in December 2025. It targets one of the biggest obstacles facing Europe’s emerging e-SAF industry: the gap between the price producers need to finance projects and what aviation fuel buyers are prepared to pay.

The intervention comes as policymakers push to translate Europe’s aviation decarbonization mandates into new production capacity.

A test for Europe’s e-SAF pipeline

Europe has built a sizeable pipeline of proposed synthetic aviation fuel projects, but many have yet to secure financing.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or EASA, says roughly 50 synthetic aviation fuel projects across the EU are awaiting final investment decisions.

For developers, securing long-term buyers remains critical. Production facilities require substantial upfront investment, while airlines and other fuel buyers have generally favored shorter contracts. They have also been reluctant to commit to higher future prices without greater certainty.

The three-country programme is designed to address that mismatch directly.

Germany will provide up to $2.4 billion, accounting for most of the funding. Austria and Luxembourg will each contribute up to $71 million.

Subsidized e-SAF volumes will be allocated among the countries according to their respective funding contributions. The programme remains subject to European Commission approval under EU state aid rules.

Double auctions tackle the price gap

The mechanism uses separate competitive auctions for e-SAF producers and buyers.

An intermediary will establish clearing prices through the two processes. Public funding will then cover the difference between the price required by producers and the amount buyers are willing to pay.

The structure is intended to provide developers with the revenue visibility needed to support investment decisions without requiring airlines to assume the entire cost premium.

Dagmar Fehler, chief executive of NOW GmbH, which is supporting Germany’s transport ministry on the programme, described the mechanism as the link between long-term investment security for producers and the shorter procurement cycles buyers typically use.

Austria’s mobility minister, Peter Hanke, said the joint funding was “sending a strong signal in favour of establishing a European market for renewable fuel,” adding that the scheme was “creating long-term prospects for producers, promoting transparent price signals and helping to ensure that e-SAF will also be available in Austria.”

RELATED ARTICLE: Argus Launches SAF Emissions Cost Indexes

The programme sits within the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation framework, which is steadily increasing sustainable aviation fuel requirements.

SAF must account for 2% of aviation fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025. That requirement rises to 6% in 2030 and 70% by 2050.

EASA data show suppliers delivered 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel at EU airports in 2025. SAF accounted for 1.1 million tonnes, or 2.8%, putting supply above the initial mandatory threshold.

Yet those figures also expose Europe’s supply-chain challenge.

Used cooking oil accounted for 80% of SAF supplied, while 85% of feedstocks originated outside the EU. E-SAF, produced using renewable hydrogen and sustainable carbon, remains a marginal part of the market.

For hydrogen developers and electrolyzer suppliers, the coalition offers a price-risk backstop in a sector where uncertain offtake has delayed investment decisions.

For governments, the programme will test whether coordinated national funding can accelerate production while the European Commission considers a broader EU financing mechanism.

The stakes extend beyond aviation. A functioning e-SAF market could create additional demand for renewable electricity, hydrogen and carbon-management infrastructure across Europe.

Success will ultimately depend on whether the auctions convert planned projects into operating capacity. If they do, the three-country model could offer Europe a practical route from aviation mandates to a more domestic, hydrogen-based fuel supply.

title: Sustainable Business Aviation : Concrete Solutions / Avico
description:
For companies using sustainable business aviation, the question has become more concrete.
Why Sustainability Is Becoming an Issue for Business Aviation Customers Business aviation occupies a specific place in corporate mobility policies.
Emissions associated with business travel fall in particular under Scope 3, within the “business travel” category of climate reporting frameworks.
How Avico Supports a More Responsible Approach A sustainable business aviation strategy also requires access to usable data.
Conclusion Sustainable business aviation does not currently rely on a single mechanism capable of completely eliminating the climate impact of a flight.
text:
Aviation remains a major challenge for companies seeking to reduce their carbon footprint. However, the issue is no longer limited to carbon offsetting. Sustainable aviation fuels, aircraft selection, load-factor optimisation and accurate emissions measurement are now among the tools available. In 2026, global SAF production is expected to reach around 2.4 million tonnes. This represents just 0.8% of total aviation fuel consumption. Therefore, the gap to large-scale deployment therefore remains considerable.

For companies using sustainable business aviation, the question has become more concrete. Procurement, finance and CSR departments increasingly seek to document the impact of business travel. They also want to identify measures that can deliver genuine results. Meanwhile, European non-financial reporting rules were revised again in 2026. The new standards aim to simplify reporting obligations while maintaining usable environmental information.

There is no single solution capable of making a private flight “carbon neutral” through an accounting mechanism alone. Instead, a credible approach involves several measures. Companies can reduce travel where possible, use lower-carbon fuels, optimise operations and account separately for residual emissions.

Why Sustainability Is Becoming an Issue for Business Aviation Customers

Business aviation occupies a specific place in corporate mobility policies. It meets requirements for productivity, connectivity and flexibility, but its emissions must now be incorporated into a broader approach to business travel.

For a company, the first step is to establish precisely what it wants to measure. Emissions associated with business travel fall in particular under Scope 3, within the “business travel” category of climate reporting frameworks. European ESRS standards also provide for the disclosure of significant Scope 3 emissions by category for companies within their scope.

Regulatory Pressure and CSRD Reporting

The CSRD has significantly changed the way large European companies approach environmental performance. The first companies concerned applied the new rules to their 2024 financial year. Their reports were then published in 2025. In July 2026, the European Commission adopted revised ESRS standards as part of the simplification of the framework.

This does not mean that all companies must now produce the same level of reporting. The scope of the CSRD has been narrowed as part of the European simplification measures. For companies that remain subject to the rules, however, the quality of environmental data is becoming increasingly important.

Business travel can therefore form part of a company’s inventory of indirect emissions. ESRS E1 identifies business travel among the Scope 3 categories to be considered when they are material.

Therefore, reliable flight data is particularly useful for companies that regularly use business aviation. It can help meet reporting requirements where applicable. It can also support an effective emissions-reduction strategy.

The first question should therefore not be “How can I offset my flights?” but rather “What is the actual footprint of my business travel and which measures can reduce it?”

Growing Expectations from Internal and External Stakeholders

Regulation is only one part of the issue. In addition, senior management, investors, customers, employees and procurement teams are paying greater attention to corporate environmental policies.

This shift is particularly visible when it comes to business travel. For example, a credible CSR policy requires a clear understanding of business travel. Companies need to know why journeys are necessary, how often they occur and how their impact is monitored.

The issue also affects corporate communications. Claiming that a journey is “zero carbon” simply because an offset has been purchased can be misleading if the emissions generated by the flight have still been released into the atmosphere.

A more robust approach is to distinguish between the different stages: measure emissions, reduce them as much as possible, then address residual emissions. This hierarchy helps prevent genuine reductions from being confused with carbon offsetting mechanisms.

Therefore, companies can build mobility policies that reflect their operational constraints. This approach is more relevant than seeking a single environmental solution for every flight.

The Concrete Solutions Available Today

Companies now have several tools at their disposal to reduce or better manage the environmental impact of business aviation. However, they do not all have the same effect.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) acts directly on the fuel’s life-cycle emissions. Aircraft selection and load-factor optimisation can reduce fuel consumption relative to the mission. Offsetting addresses residual emissions, but does not change the fact that the flight itself generated emissions.

The priority is therefore to combine the different measures rather than treat them as alternatives.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel: Availability and the Actual Additional Cost

SAF is currently one of the main immediately available tools for reducing the climate impact of air transport. The European ReFuelEU Aviation regulation requires a minimum share of SAF in fuel supplied at European airports. The requirement started at 2% from 2025 and will rise to 6% in 2030. Ultimately, the trajectory aims to reach 70% by 2050.

However, this regulation does not mean that every private flight can be refuelled with an equivalent quantity of SAF. Availability still depends on infrastructure, suppliers, airports and the operations concerned.

Globally, production remains far below projected demand. IATA estimates that in 2026, SAF will account for around 0.8% of global aviation fuel consumption. To meet long-term decarbonisation objectives, production would need to reach approximately 500 million tonnes per year by 2050.

Cost is another obstacle. Moreover, cost remains another obstacle. IATA estimates that the average price of SAF in 2025 was significantly higher than conventional fossil-based aviation fuel. Additional costs were particularly high in some regulated markets.

For a business aviation customer, SAF should therefore be considered as an option that can be incorporated into a quotation when operational availability allows. It is also important to verify the methodology used to account for the associated emissions reduction.

Across its entire life cycle, the fuel’s environmental benefit can be assessed rather than simply at the point of combustion. ICAO also provides a specific methodology for calculating the life-cycle emissions of fuels eligible under the CORSIA framework.

Avico, for its part, states that it is progressively integrating environmental criteria into its chartering decisions and offering options related to sustainable aviation fuels.

Carbon Offsetting: What It Covers and What It Does Not

Private jet carbon offsetting takes place after the flight’s emissions have been measured. In practice, companies finance projects or mechanisms designed to compensate for a specified quantity of emissions. These initiatives follow defined rules and standards.

It should not, however, be confused with physically eliminating the emissions produced by the aircraft. The CO₂ released during the flight has still entered the atmosphere.

This distinction is essential when developing a business aviation CSR strategy. However, carbon offsetting does not replace direct reductions. Companies still need to reduce fuel consumption, use lower-carbon fuels and optimise operations.

International schemes such as CORSIA also distinguish between reductions associated with the use of eligible fuels and mechanisms based on emissions units. The ICAO has established specific monitoring, reporting and verification rules for these mechanisms.

For a company, a credible approach should therefore make it possible to identify separately:

emissions generated by flights;

reductions achieved through the potential use of SAF;

residual emissions;

any carbon offsetting operations financed.

Avico offers its customers a voluntary carbon offsetting solution and states that it enables them to measure and manage their emissions as part of their CSR strategy.

The objective is therefore less about presenting a flight as “carbon neutral” than about accurately documenting what has been measured, reduced and offset.

Aircraft Selection and Load-Factor Optimisation

The third lever is operational. Not all aircraft consume the same amount of fuel, and the number of passengers carried has a significant impact on the footprint per traveller.

The environmental impact of private jets should therefore be assessed according to the actual mission. For example, an oversized aircraft may consume unnecessarily large amounts of fuel when carrying only four passengers. A better-suited aircraft can reduce this impact.

The decision should also take into account distance, number of passengers, baggage and airport constraints. The objective is not necessarily to systematically select the smallest aircraft, but rather the aircraft that best matches the actual requirement.

Load factor is another important parameter. In addition, load factor plays an important role. When several passengers share a chartered aircraft, fuel consumption is distributed across the group. As a result, the footprint per passenger decreases.

The principle is therefore straightforward: avoid unnecessary flights, choose the right aircraft and maximise its capacity wherever possible.

For companies, this approach can be integrated directly into their booking policies. Environmental performance then becomes one decision-making criterion alongside price, travel time, availability and operational constraints.

How Avico Supports a More Responsible Approach

A sustainable business aviation strategy also requires access to usable data. Without measuring emissions, it becomes difficult to compare missions, establish a trajectory or monitor progress.

Avico states that it integrates environmental criteria into its selection of charter solutions and offers mechanisms enabling customers to measure and offset their emissions.

Reporting Emissions Associated with Your Flights

Reporting is the starting point for a structured environmental policy.

For each journey, several factors can be taken into account: route, aircraft type, fuel consumption or the corresponding estimate, number of passengers and any use of SAF.

The benefit is the ability to progressively build a historical record. For example, a company operating several dozen flights per year can identify its most frequent routes. It can also analyse the aircraft used and its main sources of emissions.

This information can subsequently be compared with the data required for the company’s environmental reporting. For companies concerned by the ESRS framework, these standards require several emissions disclosures. They include gross Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions, as well as significant Scope 3 categories.

Data quality therefore becomes just as important as data volume. A clearly documented estimate is more useful for managing a CSR strategy than a global indicator whose calculation methodology is unknown.

Options Available Depending on Aircraft in the Partner Network

Not every environmental solution is available on every aircraft or route. This is particularly true of SAF, whose physical availability remains dependent on refuelling infrastructure.

Avico states that it incorporates environmental criteria into its charter selection process and offers solutions enabling customers to go further in their environmental approach.

A flight search can therefore take several criteria into account: an aircraft suited to the number of passengers, mission optimisation, the possibility of using SAF when available, and systems for monitoring or offsetting emissions.

For a company, this approach makes it possible to move from a simple “offset flight” logic towards a broader responsible business aviation strategy.

Our private jet charter service can therefore be considered while taking into account both operational constraints and the environmental objectives of the journey.

Conclusion

Sustainable business aviation does not currently rely on a single mechanism capable of completely eliminating the climate impact of a flight. The solutions available are complementary.

SAF is the main directly applicable tool for reducing the carbon impact of aviation fuel, but its availability and cost remain significant constraints. However, carbon offsetting only addresses part of the residual emissions. It does not eliminate the emissions produced during the flight. Meanwhile, aircraft selection, load factor and mission optimisation can directly reduce fuel consumption.

For companies, the first step is therefore to accurately measure their business travel. This data can then be used to establish a strategy consistent with CSR objectives and, where applicable, regulatory reporting requirements.

A credible approach ultimately follows a simple hierarchy: measure, reduce, optimise, then offset residual emissions.

text:
Methane-to-SAF pathway combines Infinium's commercially deployed advanced Fischer-Tropsch platform with electrified reforming to expand where low-carbon aviation fuel can be produced.

Infinium has introduced its mSAF product offering, a new methane-derived sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) platform which converts renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas and other qualified methane streams into low-carbon aviation fuel. The new offering expands the feedstocks and locations available for Infinium projects while complementing the company's growing CO₂-based eSAF business.

The expansion addresses a fundamental challenge for aviation: no single feedstock pathway can produce all of the low-carbon fuel needed to satisfy rising SAF mandates and industry commitments. Renewable natural gas, biogas, flare gas and other methane streams are already aggregated at landfills, dairies, wastewater facilities and gas-gathering systems across North America, Asia, Europe and other geographies and are increasingly looking for diversified end-use opportunities.

“mSAF expands what Infinium's platform can do. It gives us another way to apply our proven technology, develop projects across a broader range of locations and deliver more low-carbon fuel alongside our growing eSAF business. Aviation needs multiple scalable pathways, and Infinium is positioned to continue to deliver options,” said Robert Schuetzle, CEO of Infinium.

One proven technology, two feedstock pathways. Infinium has more than a decade of experience converting gases into liquid hydrocarbons with its synthesis technology deployed across commercial installations. Synthesize™ — Infinium's proprietary advanced Fischer-Tropsch catalyst and reactor design for converting syngas into liquid hydrocarbons — is also used to produce Infinium eFuels today. The two product lines share core synthesis technology, catalyst manufacturing, product specifications and certification pathways.

Electrified reforming improves yield and carbon performance. Infinium's mSAF platform also utilizes its proprietary Reform™ package — a proprietary electric steam methane reformer (eSMR) designed to produce syngas with a lower carbon footprint than a traditional gas-fired SMR. Today, Infinium is building the world's largest eSMR at Project Roadrunner, advancing a critical step in the conversion of methane into liquid fuels.

Conventional steam methane reforming burns a portion of the feed gas to produce process heat. This adds combustion emissions to the fuel's lifecycle footprint and consumes feedstock carbon that could otherwise be converted into the finished product.

Infinium's Reform™ technology uses renewable electricity to provide that process heat. This keeps more feedstock carbon available for conversion, increasing fuel yield per unit of gas, while avoiding the reforming-related combustion emissions associated with conventional systems. For RNG projects, where feedstock cost and carbon intensity are central to commercial performance, greater yield and lower reforming emissions directly improve project economics.

Carbon intensity verified project by project. Infinium worked with RMI, an independent energy and climate research organization with expertise in methane emissions, low-carbon fuels, aviation and industrial decarbonization, on an assessment of the growing mSAF market opportunity.

“Biogas and renewable natural gas are emerging as important areas of inquiry for hard-to-abate sectors, including low-carbon fuels and industrial value chains. These pathways may offer meaningful climate and commercial value, but only if they are supported by rigorous lifecycle accounting, auditable chain-of-custody systems, and credible certification frameworks. RMI was pleased to support Infinium's strategic assessment of this evolving landscape to better understand challenges and opportunities for meaningful climate benefit,” said Bryan Fisher, Managing Director at RMI.

The mSAF designation does not imply a single carbon-intensity value across all projects. Lifecycle emissions will depend on the methane source, leakage rate, production-energy mix and chain of custody on individual assets. Infinium will calculate and independently certify carbon intensity at the project level under applicable regulatory and voluntary certification frameworks.

By adding mSAF to its eFuels platform, Infinium is expanding the range of feedstocks and locations available for low-carbon fuel production while continuing to advance its CO₂-based eSAF business.

text:
In late August, U.S. Grains & BioProducts Council Regional Director for Taiwan Michael Lu attended the 10th New Energy International Forum, and the Council sponsored a keynote speaker to offer a global perspective on decarbonization, low-carbon fuel policies and the strategic role of biofuels in achieving net-zero objectives.

text:
The team at Seattle-based Nimbus Aerospace had planned to finish testing its quarter-scale prototype earlier in the summer, but struggled to schedule one of the few pilots skilled in remote-controlled flight.

“Not many people wanted to fly this thing,” said Adrian Groos, co-founder and CEO of Nimbus. “It was a $1 million-plus model that was significantly bigger than anything else most people have flown, as well as heavier.”

The startup is developing a hybrid-electric aircraft with high-lift wings designed to improve fuel efficiency. Nimbus plans to build a six- to eight-passenger aircraft with a 1,500-mile range that uses half as much fuel as a comparable conventional plane.

In June and August, the startup conducted two test flights of its NX1 prototype at the Pendleton Airport UAS Range in Oregon. The aircraft, which has a 15-foot wingspan and weighs 200 pounds, flew for 3 minutes 42 seconds in the first flight and 6 minutes in the second.

The tests achieved their goals of demonstrating the company’s manufacturing capabilities and the aircraft’s aerodynamics and stability, Groos said.

Nimbus has started engineering a full-scale prototype, with test flights targeted for 2028. The team is still deciding where to build the aircraft, considering Seattle against other locations around the country.

The ultimate goal is to begin delivering aircraft to customers in late 2030.

To get there, the team is working to navigate the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process as smoothly as possible. The company has built a system called the ACT (AI Certification Tool) Platform to streamline and expedite FAA certification, and a former FAA deputy director of aircraft certification sits on the startup’s advisory board.

While the Nimbus product has a unique hybrid powertrain, components such as landing gear and lights use already-approved, pre-certified parts that will also be cheaper and easier to fix.

“We’re not trying to build a super novel design. That’s just a certification nightmare,” Groos said. “We’re trying to bring an aircraft to market that solves the needs that the people are asking for.”

And what customers want is a plane that burns less fuel and requires less maintenance, he added.

Aviation is one of the most difficult industries to decarbonize. It contributes 2.5% of the greenhouse gases emitted annually, but that percentage is expected to increase as other sectors go low-carbon and air travel increases. In addition to battery- and hydrogen-powered aircraft, sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is seen as the most promising solution for larger planes.

Washington state is also home to sustainable aircraft startup magniX, though others have shut down. Electric-aviation startup Zunum Aero and Outbound Aerospace folded, and ZeroAvia largely ceased operations in the state earlier this year, though it remains active in the United Kingdom. California-based Universal Hydrogen, which test-flew a hydrogen-fueled plane in Moses Lake, Wash., closed in 2024.

“People created products that weren’t really ready for prime time,” Groos said. That’s particularly the case for hydrogen-powered aircraft — the fuel is in limited supply and the path to certification is uncharted, he added.

Other companies in the hybrid-electric space include Heart Aerospace, Electra.aero and Ampaire.

text:
Haffner Energy has secured a firm €3.2 million order from INCAD, the project company developing Quebec’s first Multi-Energy Hub in Bécancour, marking a significant step toward commercial deployment of its biomass-to-energy technology in Canada.

The contract, signed on September 25, 2026, covers six equipment units already manufactured and held in Haffner Energy’s inventory, along with associated engineering services. The remaining equipment required for the project will be manufactured in Canada under licence from Haffner Energy. Delivery of the initial equipment is planned before the end of 2026, subject to international transportation and logistics conditions.

The agreement features an accelerated payment structure. INCAD will pay a €480,000 upfront payment, equivalent to 15% of the contract value, by October 12, 2026. A further 75% of the contract price will be invoiced and received within 30 days of FOB delivery. Because the equipment being supplied has already been manufactured and paid for, Haffner Energy expects the order to generate cash inflows without significant additional industrial expenditure.

The company also expects the contract to support near-term revenue and earnings. Under its percentage-of-completion accounting approach, the allocation of already-manufactured equipment to the project could allow a substantial portion of the contract revenue to be recognised during the current financial year.

The INCAD order is separate from Haffner Energy’s broader licensing agreement with Mundi Énergies, which covers deployment of the technology across Canada. Haffner Energy has already received a €1 million upfront licensing payment and owns a 49% stake in Mundi Haffner Technologies Inc., the Quebec-based technology development company.

Located within the Bécancour Industrial and Port Park, the INCAD facility is designed to produce approximately 400 Nm³/h of renewable natural gas (RNG) from residual biomass. Commissioning is targeted for the second quarter of 2028.

The project will also produce biochar, which can be used as a soil amendment and for long-term carbon sequestration. In addition, a portion of the thermolysis oil will be used in demonstration campaigns for renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel production, supporting qualification of the SB-HEFA pathway.

INCAD is intended to become the first project in a planned network of around 20 Multi-Energy Hubs across Quebec. Future facilities are expected to operate at substantially larger capacities. The business model could provide Haffner Energy with multiple revenue streams spanning equipment sales, engineering, licensing royalties, maintenance and operations, local manufacturing and minority investments in project companies.

The companies are already preparing subsequent developments, with several potential Quebec sites progressing beyond feasibility studies toward biomass-supply arrangements. Haffner Energy said the Bécancour project will provide an industrial showcase for its technology across Canada and North America, demonstrating the conversion of biomass into RNG, biochar and liquid-fuel feedstocks.

Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact

The project should strengthen demand for residual biomass, renewable natural gas, biochar and downstream renewable-fuel feedstocks, while creating additional technology and equipment demand as similar hubs are developed. For tracked chemical commodities, the near-term impact is likely limited because the facility is not yet operational. Over the longer term, expanded RNG and renewable-fuel production could increase demand for catalysts, adsorbents, process chemicals and specialty materials used in gas upgrading and fuel processing. However, the €3.2 million order alone is unlikely to materially shift broad chemical prices; larger impacts would depend on the scale and pace of subsequent Quebec projects.

title: Ethanol industry sees maize as value-creation opportunity, not competition: AIDA

text:
Chennai: India’s ethanol industry is not competing with any particular sector for maize but is using the crop to create greater value from domestic agricultural resources while supporting energy security and rural value chains, according to All India Distillers’ Association (AIDA) Deputy Director-General Bharati Balaji.

In an email interview with BusinessLine, Balaji said ethanol production was drawing on a diversified feedstock base that includes surplus Food Corporation of India (FCI) rice, damaged foodgrains and sugar-based feedstocks, alongside maize.

She said continued improvement in maize productivity, more efficient supply chains, greater availability of alternative feedstocks and better coordination between agricultural production and industrial demand would help ensure adequate supplies for different end-use sectors.

Maize has emerged as an important ethanol feedstock as India’s domestic biofuel ecosystem expands. However, the crop also serves the food, feed and industrial sectors, meaning its prices are influenced by the overall balance between production, consumption, stocks, logistics and market demand, Balaji said.

Grain feedstocks gain significance

The increasing contribution of maize, surplus FCI rice and damaged foodgrains highlights the evolution of India’s ethanol sector into a multi-feedstock ecosystem, reducing dependence on any single agricultural resource, according to AIDA.

By the end of August, maize had contributed around 345 crore litres of ethanol, while surplus FCI rice accounted for around 214 crore litres and damaged foodgrains for around 64 crore litres.

“These volumes clearly demonstrate that alternative feedstocks are no longer marginal sources; they are becoming an important part of India’s overall ethanol supply chain,” Balaji said.

She added that the availability of multiple feedstocks could help maintain ethanol production when supplies of a particular raw material are constrained in a specific season or region. Maize, in particular, provides an additional agricultural route for ethanol production and can complement other feedstocks.

Surplus FCI rice also provides a way to utilise available foodgrain stocks, while damaged or non-food-grade grains unsuitable for human consumption can be diverted towards industrial ethanol production.

According to Balaji, this flexibility enables the ethanol industry to respond to changing agricultural conditions, improve the utilisation of domestic resources and strengthen the reliability of ethanol supplies.

Grain-based ethanol becomes major pillar

Grain-based feedstocks contributed 624 crore litres of ethanol by the end of August, accounting for nearly 70% of the 895 crore litres supplied during the period, Balaji said.

She said the figures indicate that grain-based ethanol has moved beyond its earlier role as a supplementary source and has become a major component of India’s ethanol programme.

The shift also reflects the industry’s growing diversification beyond traditional sugar-based feedstocks. Grain-based ethanol now complements ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, B-heavy molasses and C-heavy molasses, she said.

Balaji said the industry should continue focusing on maintaining a diversified feedstock base and improving coordination between procurement, production and supply.

New avenues needed for ethanol

The next phase of India’s ethanol programme will require the development of additional demand avenues alongside production capacity, Balaji said.

Flex-fuel vehicles could provide a significant mobility-linked demand avenue by enabling higher ethanol blends, while compressed biogas (CBG), sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other emerging applications could expand overall bioenergy demand.

“The key requirement will be to develop demand alongside production capacity,” she said, adding that a predictable policy environment, wider end-use adoption and investment in supporting infrastructure would be important for efficient utilisation of the capacity created by the industry.

Balaji also described the reported move towards vehicles capable of operating on 100% ethanol as a significant development, as it could allow ethanol to expand beyond conventional blending applications.

However, wider adoption would require corresponding attention to fuel availability, retail infrastructure, vehicle adoption and standards, she said.

Integrated ecosystem needed

According to AIDA, the larger opportunity lies in building an integrated ecosystem in which mobility, CBG, SAF and other applications complement the existing ethanol blending programme and provide multiple avenues for utilisation.

Balaji said the next stage of India’s ethanol journey would depend on feedstock availability, production capacity and end-use demand developing in tandem.

“The priority now should be to maintain a healthy alignment of these,” she said, adding that this would require greater productivity and diversification across agricultural feedstocks, efficient utilisation of existing distillery capacity and development of new end-use applications.

text:
Despite a 20% gain in fuel efficiency of the global commercial passenger fleet, aviation’s absolute emissions are forecast to rise 87% by 2050, forecasts aviation market intelligence company IBA. It estimates direct tailpipe emissions from passenger aircraft will rise from 843 million tonnes of CO2 in 2025 to 1,583 MtCO2 in 2050. This, points out IBA, is gross tank-to-wake emissions, so not inclusive of emissions reduction benefits from the use of sustainable aviation fuels or the application market-based measures. The rise in absolute emissions will be driven by a 134% growth in global passenger traffic, measured in revenue passenger kilometres (RPK), and expansion of the commercial aircraft fleet to more then 56,000 aircraft over the period. IBA’s NetZero platform notes a growing divergence between absolute emissions and emissions intensity.

Under its 20% fuel efficiency gain forecast, average fleetwide emissions intensity would fall from around 91gCO2/RPK in 2025 to 73gCO2/RPK by 2050, driven by fleet renewal and future aircraft delivering lower fuel burn than the aircraft they replace. However, this gain will not be sufficient to offset the effect of continued traffic growth, and the industry will be dependent on an acceleration of credible sustainable fuels and carbon removals, says IBA in its latest Sustainability Watch analysis.

“We expect fleet renewal to continue delivering meaningful improvements in emissions intensity through to 2050, but the scale of projected passenger growth means this will not be enough to reduce absolute emissions on its own,” commented Archie Brown, Senior Analyst at IBA.

“Closing the gap between this baseline outlook and the industry’s net-zero ambitions will require much greater deployment of sustainable aviation fuel, alongside further operational efficiencies and effective policy intervention. The challenge will be ensuring those measures scale quickly enough to keep pace with the continued growth of global air travel.”

Dedicated freighters are excluded from IBA’s analysis and assumes zero-emission aircraft will enter the fleet only from 2046 and account for just 0.3% of the global commercial passenger fleet by 2050, with their impact confined to local and regional travel.

IBA’s baseline scenario combines aircraft series-level delivery and retirement forecasts with projected demand, utilisation and load factors, with emissions calculated by aircraft series using efficiency assumptions for future models.

Rather than representing a net-zero pathway, the analysis provides a benchmark against which airline and industry decarbonisation strategies can be assessed, recommends IBA.

text:
Jet fuel demand in India would rise from about 192,000 barrels per day in 2024 to 277,000 barrels per day by 2031, providing a strong market for the Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), as per a report released on Monday.

The government has announced SAF blending roadmap starting with 1 per cent blending in 2027 and increasing to 2 per cent in 2028 and 5 per cent in 2030 to decarbonise the aviation industry.

The report jointly developed by S&P Global Energy and the SAF Association estimates that the SAF demand will be 46,000 tonne in 2027, which would rise to 250,000 tonne in 2030.

India's aviation sector is expected to remain one of the fastest-growing sources of refined product demand through 2060, providing a strong foundation for developing a domestic SAF market, the report said.

"This expansion is driven by rising middle-class mobility, continued growth in domestic and international air travel, airport infrastructure development, and ongoing airline fleet additions," it said.

The report, released at 2nd India SAF Conclave, noted that while some short-term weakness emerged in 2026, particularly in the international segment, the underlying demand trajectory remains firmly positive.

India's aviation fuel consumption softened in mid-2026, with July demand falling to about 180,000 barrel per day reflecting weaker flight activity, higher operating costs, and supply-side disruptions, it said.

However, first-half 2026 jet fuel consumption still increased by nearly 2 per cent year-over-year, suggesting the recent slowdown is temporary rather than structural and does not alter the longer-term growth outlook, the report said.

"The demand outlook is further supported by rising passenger traffic, the continued expansion of low-cost aviation, and increasing international connectivity," it said.

New infrastructure, including Navi Mumbai International Airport and Jewar Airport in Noida, is expected to ease capacity constraints and support additional growth in flight activity.

International aviation is likely to remain an important demand driver, with international seat capacity expanding faster than domestic capacity in 2026 despite higher ticket costs.

"Policy support is also expected to play an important role in sustaining aviation growth. A key structural driver is the government's continued focus on expanding air connectivity through UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Nagrik) Regional Connectivity Scheme," the report said.

It highlighted that the government has introduced an aviation turbine fuel (ATF) pricing stabilization mechanism, including a fixed ATF price in Delhi and a dedicated stabilization fund.

While not a direct subsidy, the mechanism reduces fuel price volatility and improves cost visibility for airlines, it added.

title: 300MW electrolyser construction starts off Spanish 'hydrogen valley' - Chemistry World
authors: Andy Extance, Rosie Rothwell, Phillip Broadwith, Julia Robinson, Mason Wakley, Maria Burke, Anthony King, Victoria Atkinson, Rebecca Trager
description:
In September, Spanish energy company Moeve started building a 300MW solar-powered electrolyser to make CO2-emission-free ‘green’ hydrogen in Huelva, in the south of the country.
This is billed as the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve has ambitions to develop to a total electrolysis capacity of 2GW.
Odenweller’s research highlights ‘ambition gaps’ between announcements about green hydrogen and reality, with many projects being abandoned.
He highlights that the Huelva plant is set to produce 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually.
Odenweller expects green hydrogen demand from the plant to remain clustered within the nearby hydrogen valley region ‘for the foreseeable future’.
text:
In September, Spanish energy company Moeve started building a 300MW solar-powered electrolyser to make CO2-emission-free ‘green’ hydrogen in Huelva, in the south of the country. The Spanish government is contributing €300 million (£260 million) towards the over €1 billion cost of the site. Moeve intends to use the hydrogen to replace some of the fossil-derived hydrogen it uses at the existing refinery onsite, as well as hydrogenating waste vegetable oils to make low-emissions liquid hydrocarbon fuels for aviation, shipping and heavy-duty road transport, and in chemical manufacturing.

This is billed as the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve has ambitions to develop to a total electrolysis capacity of 2GW. It follows similar projects in Lingen, Germany, where RWE intends to have a 300GW electrolyser operational next year, and Stegra’s 700GW plant that – once commissioned – will feed green iron and steel production in Boden, Sweden.

Adrian Odenweller from Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, Germany, calls starting to build such a large project ‘encouraging’, although there are several larger projects worldwide. ‘This project may be particularly important for Europe, to demonstrate the feasibility of producing hydrogen in renewable-rich regions such as the Iberian Peninsula, co-located with demand,’ he says.

Odenweller’s research highlights ‘ambition gaps’ between announcements about green hydrogen and reality, with many projects being abandoned. He highlights that the Huelva plant is set to produce 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually. This is only 0.45% the EU’s target for 2030, which Odenweller says ‘is clearly out of reach by now’.

Nevertheless, the project ‘is certainly an important building block in Spain and Europe’s clean hydrogen market,’ says Peter Collins, a spokesperson for industry group Hydrogen Europe. ‘The scale and significance of the project is clear for all to see, and the construction announcement shows what a strong developer can achieve – and how these ambition gaps can be closed – with clear policy frameworks and government support.’

Moeve will use a combination of dedicated solar power generation and electricity from the grid to run the plant. To produce 45,000 tonnes of hydrogen annually from a 300MW electrolysis plant would involve running it for around 7000 hours per year, Odenweller says. That will either require a very large solar plant with electricity storage to smooth out uneven generation, or taking significant electricity from the grid. Odenweller notes that from 2030 onwards, EU Renewable Fuel of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) rules will allow hydrogen production from grid energy to be classified as green through hourly matching of consumption with renewable power.

Odenweller expects green hydrogen demand from the plant to remain clustered within the nearby hydrogen valley region ‘for the foreseeable future’. Among the potential markets, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is profitable due to relatively limited supply and government mandates for increased use, allowing for premium prices that cover the higher production costs.
